utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Let us have General Blaskic brought in, please. May I have Mr. Mesic brought in, please. We have a very busy day to day. We will try to complete Mr. Mesic's testimony. Then we have another witness. Please be seated. As I said, we will try to finish with Mr. Mesic's testimony. Perhaps even two, Mr. Harmon, but certainly one. That may take quite a while. Then we have an ex parte hearing. We will try to do all of this because Mr. Mesic has to testify in another trial and the Presiding Judge of the other Trial Chamber told me that it would take up some of the afternoon, but experience has shown us that it is not always possible to do what we planned to do. So if necessary, we will sit for part of tomorrow afternoon. Mr. Nobilo, continue with your cross-examination, please. I had forgotten to say good morning to the interpreters, but I think that everybody knows that I would like to say good morning to them. Cross-examined by MR. NOBILO (continued).

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you Mr. President and good morning Mr. Mesic. Here we are to continue and I hope that I will not be very long. Yesterday we looked at a portion of the article, the interview that you gave to the Hercegovacki Tjednik, the Herzegovinan weekly. For the interpreter, it is no. 10. You said that you did not recall this interview. What we will try to do is try to read you a portion of it and see whether this is your opinion at the time and whether this was what you were talking about. For the interpreters, it is C. (Handed). This is on Nikola Koljevic. He was in Zagreb and I hope that you recall this. Here it goes. Recently Mr. Koljevic came to Sarajevo. As an explanation, he was one of the leaders of the Bosnian Serbs. In the Bosnian press, this was interpreted as an agreement with Franjo Tudjman regarding the dividing of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Is this the truth? This is your answer: this is what the little Milosevic propaganda would like to use, that is Croatia always was in a position that we should negotiate rather than wage war. We were often criticised for it because we wanted to negotiate even with Milosevic. If Mr. Milosevic comes to Zagreb and asks to talk, obviously we will talk to him. That does not mean that we divide Bosnia with him. Croatia abides by the principle that the borders are respected and that there is no division of Bosnia-Herzegovina. The citizens of Bosnia-Herzegovina are going to decide their fate on their own. We are moving on to the next question: every once in a while, Bosnian intellectuals who had recently also been called Croat intellectuals, are criticising Franjo Tudjman on his division of Bosnia-Herzegovina. How do you comment on this? Now your answer: it is the ignorance about what Franjo Tudjman really said. He said that in principle, he supported the sovereignty of Bosnia-Herzegovina and this is why he had big discussions with Mr. Alija Izetbegovic and attempt to give him arguments to win over Mr. Izetbegovic to accept at first federal concept and later, the sovereignty of Bosnia-Herzegovina because this is the only way to get rid of Yugoslavia which is no more and which Serbia is using for the realisation of its imperial interests. I believe that Bosnia waited too long, but we cannot change this now. We must solve the problem that we are facing now. That means that Franjo Tudjman never said that Bosnia-Herzegovina should be divided. But he said that he cannot leave the Croat population at anyone's mercy in Bosnia and Herzegovina. The Croat population in Bosnia-Herzegovina does not want to join any kind of Serboslavia or any small Yugoslavia. They want to have an opportunity to cooperate with Croatia in one way or another." Mr. Mesic, is this what you were saying at that time at the time when Nicola Koljevic was visiting Zagreb? Do you still say this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe that this is at variance with what I was saying at that time. As I said, I do not recall the Herzegovinan weekly and I never authorised this. I believe that this was somehow compiled. There are some things that are acceptable here, but there are some that are misconstrued, even the use of certain words which I never use.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What would you accept today that you believe is truth in this? Is it true, for instance, that the misunderstanding or ignorance about the views of Franjo Tudjman, that he was in support of the sovereignty of Bosnia-Herzegovina but wanted to protect the Croat population there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would not like to comment on this because I really do not think that it is an authentic document.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned Fikret Abdic. Is he Muslim?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe that that is how he identified himself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned the positive role of Croatia with regard to Bihac. Can you explain this, clarify this. In what way was this positive role?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Croatia helped with the liberation, that is with the breaking of the blockade of Bihac. When the Fifth Corps was threatened.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The Fifth Corps is the Fifth Corps of the Bosnian Army, for the Tribunal's information, and they helped to resist the Serb forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Excuse me. The question and answer is going a little bit fast. I notice that Mr. Nobilo asked a question that was being translated; Mr. Mesic answered before the translation was completed. Mr. Nobilo asked another question. I think for the benefit of everybody in the courtroom, if we could just wait until the interpretation is completed before the questions are asked and answered it would be very helpful. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I am sure that Mr. Nobilo agrees with this remark.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: We will try to take breaks between questions and answers. Regarding the incident when you were misunderstood to have ordered the killing of Kordic, how did you understand that Boban said he could not kill Kordic? Was he autonomous?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe that is very clear, that this is -- was taking certain liberties. I could not order the killing of Kordic, nor did I ever order this to anyone. This is a very lax interpretation. What I asked of Mate Boban was to let it pass, but he -- I believe that he was just pretending that he could not -- he could order him anything, so I guess he could have ordered him this as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well, so we are to conclude that this was not real, that he was somehow lying to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was realistic that he could order Kordic anything.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You also mentioned a humane resettlement. When you mentioned it, you said that people started talking about it. I would like to ask you where did you hear this expression? Who mentioned it, in what context? Was this an official meeting? Was this sort of something that was talked about over lunch or dinner?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I first heard of the humane resettlement during the conversations with the Bosnian leadership. Tudjman used it several times saying that this would lower the casualties and this would limit the destruction and he mentioned this several times in his public statements. Whoever gave you all these media excerpts, he can certainly find excerpts where the humane resettlement is being mentioned.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But can you explain us, what does it mean, humane resettlement? Is this something that -- when the state is giving an opportunity to move to another place?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sorry, it is going too fast.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: It is a little bit too fast.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could you slow down, please? Could the witness be asked to repeat his answer, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: My colleague is telling me that we were going too fast, so I am going to repeat it. I said, did Tudjman say -- imply to burn down five villages and people flee the sixth on their own?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think you understood me well. I think that the reasons given was to assist people. However, I have common sense. I understand very well what this is, what kind of humane resettlement it is if one has to leave one's own hometown, family, friends, property and say that he is leaving in a humane way? He is leaving because his life is threatened, because certain actions had been taken beforehand so that he had to leave. To me, humane resettlement is a euphemism for ethnic -- for genocide.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said as an example for Croat aspirations that Croat currency was introduced in Bosnia-Herzegovina in the territories controlled by Croats. I would like to ask you what currency was in force in Bosnia at that time? Was it not the Yugoslav dinar through which the financial attack was made on Bosnian Herzegovina and Croatia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. I did not express an opinion that I criticise this. I just am stating the facts, that the Croat currency was in force there as well as the German Marks. I am not objecting to it. I am just stating the facts about it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you ever heard President Tudjman say, or anyone in the Croat leadership, that in the meetings where you were present, with Bosnian representatives, that he was advocating ethnic purity, that members of other nations had to leave the areas controlled by the Croats?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The only thing I can remember is that Tudjman claimed that after this war, that about 5 per cent of Serbs will remain in Croatia. Whether he meant -- and this is a matter of speculation -- that it is because some -- a part of Serbs would voluntarily leave and go to Serbia or whether the policy would be such -- this was not stated by him, but his view was that some 5 per cent would remain, from 10 to 12 per cent before, that later 5 per cent would remain. However, this could be interpreted in another way. In order to glean what his real view was, I spoke to Bela Tonkovic who came as -- from Serbia from Vojvadina as leader of Croats there. Tudjman proposed that the Croats there swap houses and come to Croatia, that they leave Vojvadina. Tonkovic disagreed with that because he said that for centuries their homes were there, their ancestors were there, they lived in Vojvadina and they wanted to stay there. This conversation was fairly tough and I think for a while Bela Tonkovic stopped coming to Croatia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But my question was directed to Bosnian Herzegovina. In these meetings or any other official meetings or private, did Tudjman tell you that where Croats controlled territories in Bosnia-Herzegovina, the non-Croat population need to be driven out?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. He never openly stated that the non-Croat population needed to be expelled.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned dual citizenship during examination-in-chief, so my question to you is: was this meant only for Croats in Bosnia-Herzegovina or for ethnic Croats from anywhere in the world, whether they lived in the US or Australia -- could they also get dual citizenship?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct, according to our law, all ethnic Croats can receive Croat citizenship.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Next question: with respect to the dual citizenship and the electoral law, the right to vote and be elected to the Parliament, is this a right of only ethnic Croats or all citizens of Croatia so that the ethnic Croats, let us say in Australia and the US, can vote for the Croat Parliament?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. That is cheating, because the HDZ was this way to get 10 per cent of Members of Parliament, so this would be just like in a game of chess, if you have a rook, and to give you an example, as to how far this control is going, I think that one piece of information suffices. Out of all Croats who live in Australia and who have acquired Croat citizenship, so that means Melbourne, Sydney, Perth, Adelaide -- all Croats will live there and there is quite a few of them. All of them, to the last one, voted. Nobody was on any business trip. Nobody was sick. Nobody did not show up. So that means that 100 per cent of them voted, so how serious this turns out, you conclude. As far as Bosnia and Herzegovina is concerned, the moment, this regulation was passed I called the ambassador Trnka and I said: this not only destabilises Bosnia-Herzegovina, but it does huge damage to Croatia, this system of voting, so I told him to convey to the Bosnian leadership to not agree to this, to simply be against the possibility of Croats in Bosnia-Herzegovina being able to vote for the Croat Parliament, because other serious countries, and I do not consider our own one such country, enable their own citizens who happen to find themselves abroad during election to vote for the Parliament, because they pay taxes. We got citizens who are not in diaspora. They are really authentic Bosnians. Their ancestors are from there. They do not pay any taxes from Croatia and they participate in taking decisions. They affect all of us and we are the taxpayers in our country. This is why I was against it and this is why I believe that this law will be put out of force because I think this is cheating. For instance, today, in the Federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina and in Bosnia-Herzegovina, you have high officials who are members of the Croat Parliament and I can find no parallel example anywhere in the world.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I would just like to sum up. Do you agree with my contention that all Croat diaspora can vote for the Croat Parliament and not only Croats from Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, because the entire diaspora is controlled by the HDZ and this is what suits Tudjman and his party.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You held really significant positions --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Nobilo, what I would like to ask you and I think that the judges have not interrupted you often, but when you put a question, you get an answer. If you need to say: I think that this means that or this or that, this prolongs things. You have put a question; you have an answer. If, after four, five, six questions, you say, "if I understood you well", I am being a little cruel, but that is your problem, whether you understood it well or not, I am afraid. All the judges were able to understand, so it is a bit complicated. You have put three, four, five questions regarding the status of members of the ethnic group. If every time you have to say, "if I understood well", then I am afraid it is your problem if you have not understood well. That is what I wanted to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: I understand, Mr. President, but what I am I trying to do, I am posing a direct question: could the Croats outside Bosnia-Herzegovina vote for the Croat Parliament? The answer could have been yes, but Mr. Mesic finds it necessary to elaborate, and I am trying to summarise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Nobilo, I must say it is perhaps no more objective than any other summary. It is your own summary. You have questions and you can make your own conclusions. We are slowing down things. When you say, "If I understood well", I must say once again, it is up to you whether you understood or did not understand. Even the judge, if they do not understand, it is their problem. You are putting very precise questions. They are within the framework of the examination-in-chief. The witness answers them. You may then pose more precise questions, more detailed ones, but if at the end of this whole discussion we have to see whether Mr. Nobilo has understood well or not, then, I do apologise, but I am not in agreement with that at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Of course I will stand corrected by you, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: After all, yesterday you were very well-versed in questions of propaganda and I think we understand one another well.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: I understand everything that you have said, but I am trying to separate from political propaganda what is essential for this trial. But I will certainly follow your instructions. So let us go on, but please, Mr. Mesic, I would like to ask you, be kind enough in the interest of expediency to answer direct questions very briefly so as to save time. I started by saying that you indeed held very high positions and you are probably familiar with certain details far better than many of us who live there, not to mention those who did not. Could you tell us whether there is any difference within the Croat people in Bosnia-Herzegovina, something that could be called the Herzegovina wing and the Bosnian wing, and do their interests coincide and was their fate the same in the war?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, they did not have the same fate, because the majority of Croats in Croatia stayed on and a large proportion of Croats outside of Herzegovina have had, for this or that reason, to abandon their homes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you agree -- the translation is wrong. The majority of Croats in Herzegovina stayed behind and the majority of Croats outside Herzegovina abandoned their homes, but there was an error in the translation and I added, "for this or that reason, for whatever reasons". For the benefit of the transcript, do you agree that this was a misinterpretation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the examination-in-chief, you said that, due to the disastrous policies of Franjo Tudjman, and this is a free interpretation, 500,000 Croats have fled Bosnia-Herzegovina; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not only because of that. Certainly the most important reason was the Serb aggression and the other reason is the policy of Franjo Tudjman.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Out of those 500,000, was the largest number from Central Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know all the figures, but if you are asking me about that erroneous policy, I think it is sufficient to say that the Croats inside were finding themselves under siege, and were given the task -- and Miljenko Brkic can testify to this -- that they were given this task by Mate Boban, that all Croats had to resign all their positions in Bosnia-Herzegovina, even professors, who, considering the population mix, the Croats were few in number, but they had a strong intellectual grouping. There were more than 200 university professors, assistant professors and lecturers, so Miljenko Brkic asked Mate Boban, "Well, then, where shall we go from Sarajevo", because, according to him, whoever stayed in Sarajevo was a traitor. Before all the approaches were taken around Sarajevo by the Serbs and Mate said to him, "Come and stay with us at Grude. You will live like we are living." So, you see, this was a policy to withdraw the Croats from a certain area and this was confirmed to me by people from Vares. A member of the Croat People's Council, Josip Jozelic from Vares, he told me that the HVO had evacuated Croat villages due to certain arrangements that he could not go into because he did not know what was happening. So that policy contributed to the exodus and not only the Serb aggression.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you agree, then, that one could make the conclusion from what you said that the Herzegovina wing wanted to join Croatia at all cost, but as the Croat enclaves were an obstacle to them, they sought to evacuate those enclaves so that they could attach themselves to Croatia more easily; would you agree with such a conclusion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There must have been views along those lines, but I cannot enter into the details. Who gave the orders to whom, how a certain policy was implemented. These things are often more subtle than may appear at first glance. Certainly no one will issue orders which may subsequently be exposed to criticism. This is, after all, done in a different way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, could you use the example of Vares and the crimes in Stupni Do?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The people who committed the crimes in Stupni Do obviously wanted to develop fear among the Croats because of the revenge that the Bosnia acts may take, and obviously this was in someone's interest, otherwise I see no reason for a crime of such proportions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in your view, the enclaves are surrounded by Muslim territories and have no physical links with Herzegovina and Croatia. What did the Herzegovina wing want to do with those enclaves?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would not enter into those details. It is our blame, the blame of Croatia, that we entered into a conflict with the greatest victim of the Serb aggression. I am not interested whether a Croat will stay here or move there. The whole concept was wrong and, after all, Mate Boban told me, and only a couple of months before his death, he claimed that Herzegovina would join Croatia whether people liked that or not. We could tell you an anecdote. Two or three months before his death, we met at the Intercontinental in Zagreb. He invited me to have a cup of coffee with him and of course I said certainly we could have a cup of coffee together, because, after all, the two of us are former heads of state. I was the head of State of Yugoslavia and he of Herzegovina and both have disappeared. He said, "Yes, yours has disappeared, but mine is stronger by the day." I said, "Where do you intend to go?" He said, "Where do you think, except with Croatia?" Whether that was policy or whether he was just daydreaming, it is rather difficult to say today.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned an interesting example. The Croats committed a crime in Stupni Do for the Muslim Army to start taking revenge?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not say that. I said that the crime was committed in order to be able to frighten the Croats with the possible revenge of the Bosniaks. You heard very well what I said.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Of course I agree with what you said, but I want to make a comparison. You mentioned the crime in Ahmici. The Lasva Valley was surrounded by the BiH army. The Croats of Lasva Valley had no contact with Herzegovina. The Croats of Lasva Valley were an obstacle to the secession of Herzegovina from Bosnia and a crime was committed there. Is not that the same model which was intended to be used to intimidate the Croats and to have them leave the Lasva Valley?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I claim that everyone is capable of committing crimes. No nation, or rather no members of a nation are exempt from that possibility. It is only Milan Vukovic, the judge of the Supreme Court of Croatia, who claims that a Croat cannot commit a crime. I think this statement is indicative of the Supreme Court, of its leader, and the psychosis in Croatia. I am in favour of guilt being individualised on the Serb, on the Muslim and the Croat side without any exception. Therefore, I do not exclude from this anybody, anybody's tactics, anybody's actions, but guilt has to be individualised.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But would you allow that this model of Stupni Do and Vares may have been applied in the Lasva Valley and in Ahmici? Would you allow for that possibility?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not exclude any assumption, but this is something that needs to be established. The truth has to be established. I would rather you did not ask me about my assumptions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know at all how the war in the Lasva Valley started? What was the balance of forces between the Croats and the Muslims? Who had the upper hand? Do you have any information about that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not have the real information but, in fragments, I would receive reports from that area. I have my own opinion about that, but that is not important for the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned several senior officers who were in the Croat Army and later in the HVO. Let me mention those names: Petkovic, Roso, Praljak and Tolj. Were they born in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I only know that Praljak was. I do not know where Petkovic comes from, but they would appear for a while in one army and for a while in the other. How their status was regulated, I do not know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You told us that you heard rumours to the effect that Croat soldiers had waged war in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Did you speak to any single Croat soldier who told you that he was forced to go to Bosnia-Herzegovina? That he was not a volunteer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You see, many soldiers came to see me who had fought in Bosnia-Herzegovina, who were Croat soldiers. Some volunteers from Bosnia-Herzegovina also came to visit me and before that they were Croat soldiers. The mothers and fathers would come to see me, claiming that their children were not volunteers, but that they were in Bosnia-Herzegovina. So I must admit that I requested an official explanation from the Defence Minister and he claimed that there were no Croat units in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Whether there were any, I cannot tell. I was not an inspector. Nor was it up to me to establish it. But my nephew, Vladko Mesic, who was a Croat soldier, he was in Bosnia. He came back from there and he was not a volunteer in Bosnia. He was born in Slavonia. He has nothing in common with Bosnia, but he was there. You asked me for a name. I gave you one.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As the President of Parliament, the Speaker --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: The last sentence was not translated. The witness took the floor again and I did not get the translation. "I gave you a name", said the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I said, "You asked for a name and I gave you one."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you, thank you. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: So you had certain information or certain doubts, certain suspicions. Did you, as the speaker, take any steps for this matter to be investigated, because of course it is the Assembly's responsibility regarding the use of the army outside its borders. Did you form a commission? Did you put this issue on the agenda of any single meeting and all these are your responsibilities according to the rules of procedure of the Assembly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have no possibility to form any such commissions. This is only the possibility of the Assembly. I was the primus inter pares. What I could do I tried. I asked the Gojko Susak whether there were any of our units in Bosnia-Herzegovina. He said no. I asked Franjo Tudjman because, after all, people were contacting me, not only in my office, but also when I had talk shows on the radio and a woman would call me by phone; she would introduce herself and say that her son was in the Croat Army and that he was in Bosnia. I could not establish whether this was true or not. I wanted to check on it and both these people claimed that the Croat Army was not present in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Then it was up to me to accept that or not, but I had no other powers because nobody had asked Croatia for the Croat Army to go anywhere outside the Croat territory.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But, as the Speaker of Parliament, did you propose an investigating commission? Did you propose that this should be put on the Assembly agenda? Did you make any such proposals?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If the head of state tells me that there are no Croat soldiers there, what possibility do I have to propose any kind of a commission which would be accepted in the Assembly in which the HDZ has a majority? Please, let us be realistic after all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But the proposal itself would mean a great deal. May I ask for the usher's assistance now? I have another document to show. It is the Official Gazette of the Republic of Croatia where all the laws, conclusions and bylaws are published. A copy for the Registry, the Prosecution and Mr. Mesic. (Handed). It is issue no. 14, for the interpreters. We are talking about Narodne Novine, the Official Gazette of the Republic of Croatia, no. 27, dated 6th April 1993: "The House of Representatives of the Assembly of the Republic of Croatia on 26th March 1993 adopted the following conclusion." I draw your attention to conclusion no. 3. No. 3 states: "The House of Representatives applauds the policy of the President of the Republic of Croatia and the Government of the Republic of Croatia which is based also on the fact that it is in the greatest interest for Croatia for the war to be ended and a political solution to the crisis to be found in the sovereign state of Bosnia-Herzegovina." This document is signed by the President of the House of Representatives, Stjepan Mesic. Do you remember these conclusions and did you sign them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think there is no doubt about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you do confirm that. In the light of what you just said, I am asking you, you signed conclusions which were contrary to the alleged information that you were aware of?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not understand where the contradiction is. May I interpret this? It is in Croatia's interest for the war to end and for questions to be resolved politically in the sovereign state of Bosnia-Herzegovina. I was always interested in the Sovereign Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So this is, in your view, in conformity with your aspirations at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I have another document, please. I ask for the usher's assistance. This is another issue of the Official Gazette of 10th May 1993. (Handed). For the interpreters, it is document no. 15. It is issue no. 43 of the Narodne Novine of 10th May 1993 and the text of the conclusions reads: "Pursuant to Article 113 of the Rules of Procedure of the House of Representatives of the Croat Assembly, the House of Representatives of the Republic of Croatia adopted the following conclusions at its session of 30th April 1993: "(1) The Muslims and Croats, the parties to the conflict in the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina are called upon in the interests of protecting human life, the defence of their historical communality and the sovereignty of Bosnia-Herzegovina from greater Serb aggression to immediately cease all armed conflicts in the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina in accordance with the agreement signed by representatives of both peoples. "(2) The parties to the conflict who are still not abiding by the agreement signed, are called upon to deal with all outstanding problems through their civilian and military representatives. "(3) The House of Representatives of the Croat Assembly notes that the historical togetherness of the Muslims and Croats is a precondition for the survival of both peoples in the state territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina and a foundation for the preservation of the sovereignty and integrity of the state of Bosnia-Herzegovina and its future. "(4) Both peoples are called upon to join forces and resist the Serb imperialist aggression directed at exterminating both peoples and annexing Bosnia-Herzegovina to 'the Greater Serbia'. "(5) In the aim of supporting a peaceful resolution of existing differences and the preservation of the sovereignty and territorial integrity of the friendly neighbouring state of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the House of Representatives of the Croat Parliament will send a multi-party delegation on a mission of peace and goodwill." The number, dated Zagreb, 30th April 1993, the House of Representatives, the Assembly of the Republic of Croatia, the President of the House of Representatives, Stjepan Mesic. Can you verify this document as being authentic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Next text with the usher's assistance, please. It is a Declaration on the foreign policy of the Republic of Croatia and we will read only one item referring to Bosnia-Herzegovina. Document no. 16 for the interpreters. (Handed). Issue 68 of the Narodni Novine, the Official Gazette, dated 14th July 1993. The title is, "Declaration on the Foreign Policy of the Republic of Croatia", and I am reading only chapter 4: "The state integrity of the independent and sovereign internationally-recognised state of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina is supported as well as the constitutional and legal definition of the state's structure in accord with the agreement of the three constituent peoples." Signed by the President of the House of Representatives, Stjepan Mesic. This Declaration was adopted on 30th June 1993. Can you authenticate this Declaration?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We have examined and reviewed a whole series of documents, including the list of events that occurred between Bosnia-Herzegovina and the Republic of Croatia and you confirm that this was the official policy of the Republic of Croatia which was a positive one in favour of the preservation of the integrity of Bosnia-Herzegovina, but you also said there was a secret policy. I am not asking for your opinion or your conclusions, but I am asking you, what are the grounds on which you claim that Croatia had a secret policy designed to divide Bosnia-Herzegovina? What are the facts?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There are many, but I shall list just a few. If members of the Croat Parliament go to Bosnia-Herzegovina, go to Herceg-Bosna, they are photographed there wearing HVO uniforms, while at the same time being members of the Croat Parliament. Those same people in the Croat Parliament are satanising, to the limit of the permissible, the Muslims and their right to defend Bosnia-Herzegovina. Take just the statements of Vice Vukojevic in the Croat Assembly. Take the statements of Ivan Tolj, a general of both armies, about the Muslims and about Bosnia-Herzegovina. Take just the statements of my successor, Miljelovic, referring to the Muslims, what he thought about them and how he demonised the Muslims and the very possibility of the survival of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Take what was said about the Muslims in the Croat Parliament by Antun Vrdoljak, who was at the time a deputy and director of Croat television who virtually served to the Croat public what was considered to be the official state policy. Without listing other names, these are sufficient, and this brings me to my conclusion. If I say to Franjo Tudjman that the behaviour of Izetbegovic in the Croat Parliament is impermissible, his vulgarities, his fury and rage against the Muslims -- and he does not even call them always Muslim, but refers to them as "Balijas", and when I said that this was harmful for the work of the Parliament, that it undermined the integrity of Croat policy, what should I do? He was President of a committee of the Croat Parliament when he went to Herzegovina and his photograph was taken in uniform and Tudjman said to me, "Well, do something. Have him replaced as head of that committee." I called up Ivan Milas, head of the HDZ club of deputies to carry out this proposal and his response was, "Tudjman had nothing to object about the work of Izetbegovic." On the contrary, whenever I speak to him, he supports what Izetbegovic is doing and that same Izetbegovic was elected to the Croat Parliament at the last elections on the HDZ list. So I think there is no need for me to enumerate other factors serving as grounds for me to see that the policy was -- the policy of double standards, one official one and another one that had disastrous consequences for the Croats in Bosnia-Herzegovina and for the prestige of Croatia as a serious nation in the world.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just one or two final questions. You received various kinds of information being in the position that you were. Have you been able to form any opinion about our client, Mr. Blaskic? Do you perceive him as an extremist, as a moderate person? Have you ever met him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I met General Blaskic. All the information I ever received of him was always positive. What I can especially stress is that once I stepped out of -- stepped down from the position of Speaker of the Parliament and left the HDZ, I met General Blaskic. He approached me. He shook hands with me and I considered that to be a gracious act since at that time I was no longer a member of the ruling team.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And many of the people who used to greet you and shake hands with you before did not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well, just in conclusion, you are no longer a politician of the ruling party. You are now with an opposition party and, as far as I can tell, I think you are somewhere in the centre of the political spectrum. Is one of the goals of your party the removal of all HDZ from power, and Tudjman, and do you believe that such a process would signal democratisation in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If you want my personal opinion, the Croat People's Party believes that we have replaced a single party system, which was the Communist Party system which did not allow any democratic processes to take hold, and if these democratic processes did happen, they were of short breath and it took a very long time for them to happen. But when the HDZ came into power, even though I was part of that, I disagreed with it in a sense that it again assumed control of the legislative executive power, the media, and again established a monopoly of a single part or of a single movement. In order to change that, it is necessary to either create a new movement and then face the same problem which would be retrograde. We believe that we need several parties, regardless of how strong individually they are. I believe that we need to participate in the political process, that they should go to elections and that eventually they should win. We had elections in the Oljeka Jupanja and we went to elections for the municipal bodies in my town of Orahovica, and there were two lists fielded in this election. I was leading one and the other one was led by Franjo Tudjman, and a pro-fascist Croat party of the right led by Mr. Djapic and they are known by such things as -- for instance, about a month ago, they visited Vukovar in about 100 black limousines with black shirts, black flags, and singing songs from World War II with fascist salutes and with black thoughts in their minds. So this is the coalition partner of the HDZ. However, fortunately, we, the united opposition, won and I believe that we will win in the next elections, if you are interested in that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, I am interested in that. You believe in the victory over the HDZ and Franjo Tudjman?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Do not be fooled by the composition of the Croat Parliament. The next elections will show the foolishness of it and we will meet again and you will be proud that you were once a member of my party.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you believe that it would be a great watershed, a great cross-roads if this happened?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I am afraid that this discussion, which is certainly interested, does not really concern the Trial Chamber. Have you finished, Mr. Nobilo?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Mr. President, I have concluded, but I believe there is a direct connection there. Thank you, but I have concluded.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I just understand that Mr. Mesic is recruiting members.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I already have members.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: I have completed my cross-examination. I thought it was important to note that Mr. Mesic had certain political aims, he had them in 1992-93. He has them today, but I should now like to tender into evidence the videotape with the French and English translation. That is one exhibit. Then also the Official Gazettes. These are the last three that I referred to. If Mr. Dubuisson could help me with the numbers, the one dated 10th May 1993, the other one of 6th April 1993 and of 14th July 1993. Four exhibits that I should like to tender, three issues of the Official Gazette and one videotape with the transcript translated into French and English. Mr. Prosecutor, you no longer have the same objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: There was a newspaper that was not authenticated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well. I have just been told what has been requested and what has not. Perhaps the Prosecutor has certain additional questions to put to the witness. It is his right to re-examine, after which the judges may have some questions for the witness. Mr. Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Mr. President. Mr. Mesic, you were asked questions about various conversations you had with Mr. Boban. Can you tell the Chamber how he referred to Muslims in those conversations?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I knew Mr. Boban since about 1967, 1968. We were fairly close, which is why I mentioned my discussions with him. However, after the conflict with Muslims -- and I had not noticed this before about him, he never called them Muslims. He always used an ugly expression. He called them Balijus, in a sense that we could not get along with the Balijus and that co-existence with them was impossible and we needed to part ways.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very briefly, can you describe to the judges what the term "Baliju" means? Is it a perjorative term?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as the information that I possess, it is an expression from the Turkish days and it referred to the lowest stratum of -- let us say something that would be akin to the lumpen proletariat.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now I would like to turn your attention to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Excuse me, because you know this is being translated. The lowest strata of society? We cannot use "the lumpen proletariat". How would you translate that? The serf proletariat. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Something like that. Something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: How did President Tudjman characterise President Izetbegovic and his political views?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe that President Tudjman did not know Mr. Izetbegovic very well and I -- if you allow me, I believe that I knew him somewhat better because we were represented by the same lawyer, same attorney in the previous regime. When he came out of prison and when I came out of prison, we met and I can tell you that we had friendly relations. I believe that President Tudjman was mistaken by placing President Izetbegovic among the Muslim fundamentalists. I believe that Mr. Izetbegovic is a truly religious man. I think that he is a moral person. I think that he is a wise man. He entered politics without any major previous political experience. He certainly knew what was done in politics and what politicians were doing to one another, and maybe this is why he could -- he was a bit awkward at first, but he was a moral person, an honest person and a wise person, and I think that this is a fitting description of him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was he a moderate in your view?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe that he was moderate and let me tell you --

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Mr. President, I thought of raising an objection earlier on, but I changed my mind. I never asked a single question about Mr. Alija Izetbegovic. I had planned to do it, but I thought it was not important, so I simply did not ask a single question about Alija Izetbegovic, so I think I am entitled to object to these questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes, but I was going to add that you are asking a question regarding the political opinions of Alija Izetbegovic, so please proceed to your next question.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Mr. Nobilo asked you a question in respect of whether Muslims refugees from Bosnia were housed and fed in Croatia. My question is: did the State of Croatia receive foreign aid and assistance in respect of housing and feeding those refugees and could you describe the types of foreign aid that Croatia received?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is true. A large number of refugees were in Croatia and there were a -- they were a great burden. It was both in terms of accommodation and in feeding and organising life for these refugees, for these displaced persons. And Croatia needed the donors' assistance. I do not know what amount of assistance it was. I know that there was never an objection that this food and everything else that was needed for the refugees was not sufficient. That means that, both in terms of money and food, this assistance was actually sufficient in real terms.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You also testified yesterday that one high state official from the State of Croatia said, and I quote: "We must make life so unbearable for them that they will want to leave." First of all, who made that statement? Which high state official made that particular statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I must give you the context within which this was done and then if you insist, I can tell you who it was who stated it. When the war broke out between Bosnia and Croats, when the armed conflict started and when victims started piling up, there was a great pressure in Croatia and great criticism of the Croat authorities about why they were keeping Bosnian refugees in Croat camps. And the Minister of Social Affairs at that time, Mate Granic, who now is the Minister of Foreign Affairs, said that such an impossible situation would be created for them that they would have to leave, so that other countries would receive them and that they would not be a burden on Croatia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you were asked a series of questions by Mr. Nobilo about whether Croatia was a transit country through which both humanitarian aid and weapons went into Bosnia. You said that, yes, that in fact was the case, but that Croatia itself kept a portion of the arms and the humanitarian aid as the price for permitting the transit to take place. Have I fairly characterised your answer to yesterday's question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Since this is a closed session, then maybe we can say certain things that would not go out in public, otherwise I would not dare say so. We were under an embargo, so we were not supposed to receive any arms. However, yes, we had to get arms, both we and Bosnians, because it was an absurd situation. We were victims of an aggression and we had an embargo on import of weapons. In other words, we would be just served on a matter to the Serbs that way. So the assistance did come and there was always agreement on how much of this was to be left to Croatia, both because of the needs and the risks that Croatia was taking because of the embargo. On one occasion -- actually, on more than one occasion, I asked Alija Izetbegovic whether he was satisfied with this kind of arrangement. He said, "I would be satisfied if another portion did not stay behind in Herzegovina." Which portion of that stayed behind, the amount, I too I do not know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you any idea and are you able to tell the Trial Chamber what percentage of the arms that transmitted through Croatia were taken by Croatia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is hard for me so say, because there were different arrangements. There were different sources of this material. It would be somewhere between 10 and 20 per cent.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know what happened to the arms and the humanitarian aid once it transmitted through Croatia and went into Herzegovina-Bosnia? Did the authorities there also extract a share of the arms intended for the Bosnian central Government?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, there were such occurrences.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I believe you testified that -- to put it into context -- Mr. Izetbegovic's statement to you about how much arms he received, you cited an example in yesterday's testimony that in fact there were occasions that you knew of when arms intended for relief in the siege of Sarajevo did not make it to Sarajevo because they were interdicted in Vukovar by the HDO?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Please limit yourself to the cross-examination, Mr. Harmon. Let us not restart the examination-in-chief. Thank you. Go on to another question, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: My last question: in the course of the cross-examination, it has been suggested by the cross-examination that because you are a politician in Croatia and because you oppose President Tudjman in the political arena, that your testimony in The Hague in closed session is politically motivated. Do you care to comment on that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Objectively speaking, by this testimony, I am only going to suffer political damage. I do not have any -- I do not benefit from this and since this is a closed session, this is going to be my approach for the public too. I accept the rules of this court and after this testimony I am not -- I am going to observe the rules and I am not going to interpret what the other side or a third side or somebody outside may offer, but if somebody wanted to use my testimony in political ways, it is Mr. Tudjman. When I gave my first statement to the investigators of the Tribunal, and I had to do it because there is a law in Croatia which calls for cooperation with the Tribunal, and as a legalist I abide by that and I testify about what I know. However, Mr. Tudjman somehow got the record of my statement to the investigators. He brought the media -- representatives of the media that he controls and all this was then splashed all over the media and offered to the public, because other witnesses needed to be intimidated by my being accused for high treason. You have to bear in mind that last month, during the Congress of his party, its President said, and this could only have referred to me -- he never named me, my name -- he said, "In the union protests, which was organised by four unions, which was set for the main square in Zagreb, 12,000 policemen came out to suppress this manifestation organised by the unions", and I was in the organising committee of this protest. And his Congress, President Tudjman said, "In the organising committee of this union protest, there are persons who testify and slander Croatia in The Hague. I thank him for addressing me in the plural, because that means that is a sign of respect that he has of me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Mesic. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you. Judge Riad.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Mesic. I would like to ask you first a specific question. Do you have any knowledge of the concrete position of Colonel Blaskic in the Lasva Valley? Was he, to your knowledge, the undisputed commander of the area or was it some kind of divided and anarchic region?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot say unequivocally what position and what chain of command -- where in the chain of command General Blaskic was. I only know that he was a military man, that he was in the HVO, that he was a professional soldier, and people whom I met told me positive things about him. But I do not know his place in the chain of command.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You spoke of the HVO. The HVO was disciplined, military division or was there some kind of insubordination and lack of authority throughout the various levels of commanding?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Since this army was being established in a chaotic situation, it is certain that these lines of communication did not function fully. But, in my view, this army, compared in relation to Croatia and its Ministry of Defence, it was in a subordinate position, so I assumed that the orders on many operations came from there, because oftentimes the operations of the Croat Army were coordinated with those of the HVO.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you think the policy was determined by the high authority in Zagreb and it was executed in the Lasva Valley?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My views are based on what I know and Mate Boban, as President of the HDZ and President of the Croat community of Herzegovina-Bosnia, always claimed that he was exclusively implementing the Zagreb policy and that he did not have his own policy and Zagreb meant the top of the Croat leadership.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned during your testimony that once in a discussion with Markovic, he mentioned that there was no official decision for cleansing of the Muslims, but he told you in practice they managed to make sure that no Muslim was left. Did you understand how this came to happen? Was it through terrorising the population in order to run away or was it through -- not to say genocide, but at least killing and extermination? Do you have any idea how they managed to have no Muslim left, according to Mr. Markovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Pero Markovic?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is one example, but it was known that after the conflict between Bosniak Muslims and Croats, many Bosniks who were in the HVO were disarmed and many of them ended up in camps. It is known that in many towns, there were -- pressure was exerted so that people were leaving, but the most important example to me was the one of Mostar when I sent a delegation which was going to find facts about what was going on there and, upon their return, they told me that there were a large number of Muslims from the surrounding villages, villages surrounding Mostar, and that they came into the city, so that the demographic complexion changed, not by their own will. They had to come. They were forced to come to Mostar. So now that this ethnic balance changed, which would have changed after the war because everybody would go back to where they came from, there was additional pressure to expel these people out of Mostar during the war and the television broadcast this and this was clear to everyone. If people were taken away in columns of trucks, they were not doing it because they wanted that. It was because they were pressured into doing so. That is when I asked the mayor of Capljina, Pero Markovic. I asked him what was the relations between Muslims and Croats there. I do not know what the percentages were, but the percentage of Bosniks in Capljina was, I think, maybe 5 or 6 per cent. I may be wrong, but I know that it was a small percentage. He said we have no conflicts because we cleansed them all. Cleansed in what way? It was obvious that people left under pressure. I do not know what the situation is there now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Just a more general question. You said that Mr. Tudjman was openly in favour of the frontiers established in Banovina in 1938, if I understood rightly, and this was reiterated in the meeting of Karadordevo between Tudjman and Milosevic. What was the place of the Lasva Valley in this map which was already started in Banovina? Where would the Lasva Valley go and what was the general idea about it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Tudjman believed that this was the greatest achievement the Croats had. That is, the greatest achievement of the Croats were the borders from the Banovina times. Whether that was true or not, but that was what he said after Karadordevo, that Bosnia could survive, that we would get the Banovina borders, plus Cazin, Kladusa and Bihac. As for this part, I think it was also encompassed by the former Banovina. That is, it was within the Banovina borders, the Lasva River valley.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So it was supposed to belong to Croatia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. That is what I think when I look at the map.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in that case, you would apply the humane -- what you called the -- what was the word? The humane transfer of people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. It is called humane transfer or resettlement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Judge Shahabuddeen?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Mr. Mesic, would I be right in supposing that in Croatia, there were other Croats who, like you, opposed the use of force by Croats against Muslims in Herceg-Bosna?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is the main difference between the opposition in Serbia and the opposition in Croatia. The Serb opposition, or the relevant part. I must admit, for the sake of truth, there are many honourable people. There are groups that are against the formation of a greater Serbia, against the war, against Milosevic's policy. But the radical, the relevant opposition, the radicals and how else they call themselves, Draskovic's party, they are all reproaching Milosevic for not having achieved his war goals. So there is not any great difference amongst them. They are attacking Milosevic because he failed to achieve a Greater Serbia. On the other hand, in Croatia, the opposition is criticising the Government for allowing the conflict to break out between the Croats and the Bosniaks. The position was, let us not try and pinpoint the culprits, but let us put an end to that conflict as soon as possible and go forward. People like me, who were against such a conflict, are quite numerous, in my opinion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now let us pass to this question as to whether you personally witnessed the making of any official decision for the use of force by Croats against Muslims in Herzeg-Bosna. Would I be understanding your position to be this, that, no, you did not personally witness the making of any such decision, but that you held important positions and you were in touch with important persons within the leadership, in that your understanding was that they collectively understood it to be the policy of Croatia to sanction the use of force by Croats against Muslims in Herzeg-Bosna?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I must explicitly say that I was never present when a decision was taken on the use of force by Croatia against the Bosniaks, but I must also add, that when the crime in Ahmici was committed, because I was in touch with Mate Boban, I said to him, "Tell me, because the crime is great. Have you conducted an investigation to find out who did it?" He said, "Yes, we did, and we established that the people who did it wore black uniforms". I then asked, "I did not ask you what colour uniforms they wore, but who wore those uniforms?" And he said, "They could have even been Serbs." As far as I am familiar with that part of the country, he either does not know or he did not conduct an investigation or he was lying.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could I revert to one little aspect of my question? That is, whether the impression you collected from other members within the leadership was that it was in fact the policy of Croatia to use force against Muslims in Herzeg-Bosna.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: One could have come to such a conclusion, at least I did, on the basis of a number of events, but one is particularly impressive. There was a military formation in Bosnia-Herzegovina called HOS, H-O-S, which included both Bosniaks and Croats and they fought together against the aggressor. At one point in time, an assassination was organised of General Blaz Kraljevic, who was the commander of those forces. His escort consisted of almost half Muslims, half Croats. I do not know the exact number. They were killed on a road. They were ambushed and liquidated. I never heard who accounted for that crime.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could I go to this other aspect? Defence counsel -- and I am sure you appreciate this -- as was his duty, examined you as to the relationship between the statements you are now making in court and various statements which you made while the conflict was in progress. Now, would I be correct that in your political experience, there is such an idea as not rocking the boat. That is to say, that a senior political figure would have to hold the balance very prudently between allegiance to the policy officially set and his private convictions. Have you encountered that sort of feeling in the course of your political life?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: One thing is certainly true, that I persistently advocated the Defence of Bosnia. Not only by the Bosniaks, but by the Serbs and the Croats who wanted Bosnia-Herzegovina, because that was the only chance for it to survive. Because I was convinced that if Milosevic succeeded in breaking up Bosnia, that would be tragic for Croatia, because regardless of all agreements, it is highly questionable whether Croatia could have survived or whether Greater Serbia would have been formed, even at the expense of our own territories. So that when I held a high position in the HDZ and in the Government, I always apparently accepted the official policies which were in favour of the survival of Bosnia, but I also always underlined that there has to be cooperation, that there must not be anymore war, that we should have a joint command between the HVO and the BiH army, which I think has still not been fully realised, because only such a single command can ensure a victory in a war with minimum casualties, because if there are several commands, the consequences are always tragic. Finally, let me try and summarise. I was an advocate of a united resistance against the aggressor. I was for a unified Bosnia-Herzegovina, but as a senior official, I could not directly clash, though it could have been seen from my interviews so that President Tudjman, in December 1993, proposed that I should resign my post as Speaker of Parliament, that I should go to Grenoble or to Spa for a couple of months, Spa in Belgium, for additional study of the French language, and to choose whatever ambassadorial post I wanted, because he could not come to any kind of agreement with Milosevic while I was at the head of Parliament, because I had said that he had to hang. Namely, this was something I told Milosevic in his face, that the Serbs would hang him at the main square in Belgrade at Terazije when they failed to achieve their wartime goals, which he had advocated because he had planned the war. I also asked him, when hanging, to think of me and that I would think of him. I stated that in public, but obviously this bothered him so much that he must have pressurised Tudjman to remove me from this high position and after some time, I actually did leave.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me put it this way and as simply as I can. In this closed session and before this court, do you feel freer to speak your mind than during the troubled years when there was conflict between Croats and Muslims in Herzeg-Bosna?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, certainly I feel freer here, but life in Croatia in those days did not have a very high price.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: May I ask you this question, which may seem redundant to you, but which is important to the court: are you saying to the court that your testimony today is the truth?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is the truth.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: May I ask you a little question about what I shall call the dual track policy of Croatia, which you have described. That is, on the one hand, there would be formal proclamations by the Croat authorities respecting the territorial integrity of Bosnia-Herzegovina. On the other hand, there would be a policy of seeking to divide that country. Should I understand you this way, that in the judgement of the Croat authorities, the successful implementation of the policy of division depended on continued assertion of the policy respecting the territorial integrity of the country?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: True. In that way, the Croat official policy managed to side-step criticism of the international community because it publicly supported the survival of a sovereign state, whereas the other track was in the opposite direction. To take just one example, Fikret Abdic, who was also trying to break up Bosnia-Herzegovina because he proclaimed Western Bosnia as an autonomous region without this having any grounds in the constitution of Bosnia-Herzegovina. He spent most of his time in Zagreb, but at the same time, he had contacts with Milosevic and his regime. He would purchase vast quantities of gas, allegedly for his own needs, from firms in Zagreb, and it was clear that he was selling that same oil to our common aggressor. So if we look at this mosaic, then the whole picture appears quite different from what it may appear and what it is proclaimed to be in public.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me ask you this other question which concerns the transit of arms through Croatia and Herceg-Bosna to Sarajevo. Would I be understanding you correctly to mean this, that from the perception of the Croat governmental authorities, it was to the advantage of Croatia that Bosnia-Herzegovina should continue to resist the Serbs militarily?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, this is a matter which has several layers to it. It was impossible to stop assisting Bosnia-Herzegovina because it would have been accused by everyone who supported Croatia's independence, on the grounds that it was not supporting another sovereign state, and thereby its policies would be compromised. But now that that aid was being given, it had to be reduced to such a level that it would not hinder the fulfilment of Croat political goals, so, you see, a balance had to be struck and the aid came from various quarters.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would I be correct in understanding you to mean this, that to the extent that Croatia permitted the transit of arms to Bosnia-Herzegovina, the transit of arms so effected, accorded with the interests of the Government of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I would not say the Government. I would rather say that part of the policy which had double tracks, because it was possible to measure how much aid should be given without damaging Croatia, while at the same time being in contact with the international factors which wanted the survival of Bosnia-Herzegovina and which pinpointed the main problems in those areas.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You are quite correct in qualifying my question by limiting it to the second of the two tracks. Here is my last question. It concerns your position as Speaker. You remember Defence counsel was asking you whether, as Speaker, it was not your duty to put on the agenda of the House of Representatives an item concerning the service rendered by Croat soldiers within the Croat community across the border. I am a little unclear. You would understand why I am unclear as to what exactly were the rules of procedure in the House of Representatives. Would I be right in supposing -- I may well be wrong -- that where a substantive item was concerned, that item could only be discussed on a motion made from the floor and not on the initiative of the Speaker. As I said, I may be wrong, but I do not know.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The actual procedure for putting an item on the agenda was such that the initiative would come from the Government, through the parliamentary commissions, to the President of the Assembly, the Speaker. And, after a certain time period, it was up to him to put it on the agenda. The other possibility would be for committees of the Parliament to reach the conclusion to have an item placed on the agenda and then again, with a certain time period, if this is approved, that item would appear on the agenda. A deputy himself could propose something to be put on the agenda, but then again, he had to go through this procedure, either to go through the Government and hear its opinion, or through the parliamentary committees, who would then put it on the agenda. But since in the parliamentary committees and in the Government, the majority was held by the party in power, they would halt such a procedure or such an item if it were not quite in accord with the official policy. Therefore, no matter how much we might insist in Parliament that foreign affairs be placed on the agenda, Croatia's policy towards Bosnia-Herzegovina, events there, et cetera, things would not pass this filter and it was simply not possible to put such items on the agenda in this way because this filter, that is the monopoly of power, prevented a public debate. So, you see, to this day, the issue of the state audit of financial expenditures of a number of ministries has not been put on the agenda. It is simply not possible. So the ministries have no control over them and their spending.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: I am obliged to you, Mr. Mesic. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Mesic, I am going to keep you for a few more moments, not ask questions which were already asked, but to make sure that you might be able to leave before lunch time. So if you could answer me relatively quickly. Of course, answer as you feel you have to. The Vance-Owen Plan was not ratified by the Assembly. What was your opinion? What was your influence over Mr. Tudjman? How do you see this? Could you tell us this quickly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Vance-Owen Plan was not adopted by the Serb side. They signed it, but the Serb Assembly did not adopt it. There was a deadline by which they had to sign it and they did not and the Croat and the Bosnian side accepted it, but I think that it was lucky for Bosnia-Herzegovina that it was not accepted, because it had contributed to the grouping of populations and their movement from one part to another.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was your opinion? Did you think it was a good thing? The plan, I mean.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I must say that I personally was against the plan, because I forecast how it would end. Even though I had hoped that the people would dilute the plan, in the sense that all three peoples would remain constituent peoples in all the cantons. That would be a kind of control mechanism, because if in each of the entities, all three were constituent, then this would be salvation for Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. In another area, you said that there was no official budgetary envelope for any assistance that could be given to Bosnia-Herzegovina. Do you have any idea what the actual budgetary circuits were, the parallel circuits were -- I suppose they were parallel.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Since I personally was always very well informed regarding the budget, because, after all, the most important act of any state is the law and the budget, because it determines how funds are spent. But I can claim to this day that there is not a single item in the Croat budget. At least I am not aware of it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I understood that. I was asking you something else.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was no evidence of any sums being spent in Herceg-Bosna or anywhere else. The only possibility was for the Defence Ministry to spend funds out of its own budget, but that ministry was not under our control. The Ministry of the Interior could be financing the police. The Ministry of Health, the health. The Ministry of Education, the education in another state.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You do not have to say anything else. I would just like to say that in the position that you occupied, that you should have known that the Ministry of Defence would have to also vote the budget, like in all budgets of ministries throughout the world. Well, it does not really matter. As regards the leaders of the Bosnia Croats -- perhaps they worked with General Blaskic or perhaps he was one of them. What did they come to do and if they were coming for orders, was there an idea of a joint command that was ever mentioned at the time of the war?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They certainly came for orders, because that was the only way to explain it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was the question of a more official command ever raised?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The command could only have been in Zagreb, because we know that when joint operations were conducted, everything was done within the framework of the Croat leadership.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In other words, are you now saying that General Blaskic was getting his orders from the Croat military command?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know who General Blaskic received orders from, but Mate Boban certainly received his orders from Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You also said about an article in Globus that at no point did we plan for a war against the Muslims. When you say "we", it was when you were part of the most official structures. You said at least officially we never planned for war. Was it ever planned unofficially? Do you know something about that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What I had meant was that the state leadership consisting of the legislative and executive power and also the political leadership, never had such a topic on which we could officially voice an opinion, but the only possibility was that talks and agreements may have been made that I did not participate in, because the people who came to Zagreb did not always go to those addresses where it would have been logical for them to go. To be more concrete, if in 1992 I was President of the executive board of HDZ and a delegation of the HDZ is coming from --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What month in 1992? What month was it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The whole of 1992 until the very end. And a delegation comes to Zagreb, they never came to see me in the party, because I was there professionally. As of January 1st 1992, I was physically on the premises of the HDZ, but they never came to see me. They always went to see President Tudjman. So I had this same complaint when I was in Belgrade, when Jovic met with representatives of Serbs in Croatia, especially with Milan Babic, the President of the so-called Krajina. He never came to see me. He always went to see Bora Jovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Exactly at what point do you situate your change of political position? I am not talking about Mr. Tudjman who in December of 1993 said that you would be a wonderful ambassador in a country somewhere far from Croatia. But at what point? You said, "All of a sudden, I could no longer keep my position. I was not in the official spheres. I was against the positions there." At what point do you situate this profound internal change?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is a time that cannot be actually pinpointed as a date. It is a period in which a decision matures. Most people in other parties were my friends even before the democratic changes. With some of them, I had been in gaol. I had socialised with some of them within opposition circles during the former regime and they now belonged to different parties, but I continued to be friends with them regardless. However, such a structuring of the HDZ developed as if those who were not members were not good Croats, as if they were not patriots. The HDZ started to become sufficient for its.
