Everyone else was no longer just in opposition to the HDZ, but they were enemies of the state. This is something that I could not stand. I was also bothered by the excessive centralisation. The Minister of Police, for instance, would decide where the sheriff in any outlandish municipality -- who would be there. When the Minister of Health decides who the director of a health centre will be; when the Minister of Education decides who will be the principal in every school. All of this bothered me, but the dot on the "i" was, after all, the policy towards Bosnia-Herzegovina. I thought that this was disastrous for Croatia. That, in my view, was the line when I split from the official policy.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I have the feeling you always divided between the official position. Mr. Nobilo showed this in all the articles that he cited. Then this other position which you yourself said was a kind of slow evolution. Finally, what was your real contribution to this underground position, the influence that became less and less important. But do you have any specific concrete facts or concrete things that can show us that while you may have said to Globus that you supported the official position, that actually you did not. Did you have any concrete facts? It is important for the Tribunal to know what is the profound credibility of a testimony which is so difficult to perceive. I am not trying to criticise you at all. I understand that in this tragic situation it is easy to make analysis after the fact than before or during, but the Tribunal would like to know what you concretely did, even for the Muslims. What did you do concretely? Did you say at any point in private discussions with Mr. Tudjman, "This is not acceptable. It cannot go on like this. I am going to resign publicly." Did you do something like that or was it a kind of lofty influence that you might have had? If you do not want to answer, you do not have to.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not only subtle influence. There were many debates with President Tudjman when he tried -- or, actually, I was very popular, which I must say that I personally did not like. And Tudjman wanted to have him on his side, and that is why he kept persuading me to stay on in politics, that politics needed me, but I was parting ways with those policies. I had several talks with him and he kept saying to me, how come I do not understand the Bosnian situation? How come I cannot understand what it is he wants in Bosnia-Herzegovina? In these debates of ours, each one of us had his own threshold as to how far he could go. That I did not stand by and watch is proven by the fact that 23 deputies promised to resign from the Parliament, but only 11 actually did, which means that I tried to win support from within to change the attitude towards Bosnia-Herzegovina. This policy of mine was understood by representatives of Bosnia-Herzegovina. They would meet with me, both Silajdzic and Alija Izetbegovic, and many representatives of Bosnia-Herzegovina, when they came to, Zagreb, they would always come to visit me because they realised that I was struggling for a different kind of policy, for a different relationship towards Bosnia-Herzegovina. To be even more specific, before leaving for his visit with the Pope, Alija Izetbegovic sent me a message by telephone that he would like to meet with me and that he would like me to organise a meeting with President Tudjman for him. I said I would be glad to do that, but President Tudjman is on a visit to China and he is coming back tomorrow. He said, "Fine, I will come with the Prime Minister, Silajdzic, tomorrow to Zagreb and, please, when you meet Tudjman, tell him I want to talk to him, because you usually go and meet him." We ended that telephone conversation. The two of them came to Zagreb and together with my deputies, we sat down in my office and he said the following: "I have three proposals for Franjo Tudjman. One is that the Bosnian side replace all those commanders in the Bosnian Army which is requested by the Croat side in Bosnia, on condition that the Croat side also replace the commanders who have compromised themselves in Bosnia as requested by the Bosnian side". The second proposal was for Croatia to sign an agreement and to do everything it can through the preliminary proceedings for a confederation between Bosnia-Herzegovina and Croatia. A third proposal was that the Croat General, Martin Spegelj, should take over command over the Bosnian Army to show that they were not fundamentalists, but that they were struggling for the survival of Bosnia-Herzegovina and they trusted him as a professional. So I am telling you this because these were the kind of topics they came to discuss with me because they recognised this double track policy.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. I have a last question which refers back to some of the questions that Judge Shahabuddeen asked, but looking at things from a different angle. If you were to give an interview after this testimony, once you have returned home, would you consider that you failed in your obligations toward the Tribunal? In other words, would you say, "I simply will not give any interviews once I get back", having to do with this testimony, of course.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My opinion is that my obligation to cooperate with The Hague Tribunal should not have been politicised. This was done by others, I must say at my expense, but also at the expense of the convincingness of Croatia. Since we have here agreed that I should testify in closed session, it is my obligation not to comment on what was said at this closed session. As for what happens in open session, that I am free to comment on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I have no further questions, but I believe that Judge Riad wanted to ask a question. I would like to apologise to the interpreters, but at the suggestion of my -- that is to say we will begin again at 2.45. I would like to thank you, Mr. Mesic. It was important and historical testimony. You occupied very important positions and the Tribunal must have as complete as vision as possible about what happened in respect of General Blaskic's responsibilities. These are command responsibilities. You did this and the Tribunal is appreciative to you for your cooperation and hopes it will not turn against you, but that, on your side, you will not provoke any possibilities that this would turn against you. Each side has to do its best. The Tribunal has assured you the best protection as possible. You must do the same. Having said this, the judges would like to thank you for your contribution. We will now suspend the hearing and resume at 2.45. (1.30 pm) (A short adjournment) (Open session) (2.52pm) (The accused entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon, who is the next witness, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. President, your Honours, and counsel. Our next witness is Mr. Paddy Ashdown.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: In accordance with what we always do, please tell the Trial Chamber what the main points of this testimony are, and how this testimony fits into the principal counts in the indictment against General Blaskic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Ashdown will first of all at my request testify about his professional background. Mr. Ashdown is a Member of Parliament in the UK and he is the Leader of the Liberal Democratic Party in that country. He will first summarise his experiences in the Former Yugoslavia and then he will testify about a conversation that he had with President Franjo Tudjman on 6 May 1995. The Prosecutor will present as evidence a copy of a map that was drawn by President Tudjman and annotations that were made by Mr. Ashdown. Mr. President and your Honours, his testimony is relevant to paragraphs 5.0 and 5.1 of the indictment, which allege the existence of an international armed conflict, and it is relevant to all grave breaches counts in the indictment, that is counts 5, 8, 11, 15, 17 and 19.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well. If I understood what you have just said, the testimony will deal more specifically with the conversations that the witness had with Mr. Franjo Tudjman; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: That is correct, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: And that you will focus on whether or not there was an international armed conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Correct, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well. If there are no further questions from my colleagues, thank you, we can have the usher introduce Mr. Paddy Ashdown, who, if I am correct, has not requested any specific type of protective measures; is that true?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: That is true.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you. (The witness entered court) JEREMY JOHN DURHAM (PADDY) ASHDOWN

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Do you hear me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Please, could you tell the Tribunal what your name and your given name is?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My name is Jeremy John Durham Ashdown. My -- I go by the nickname of Paddy Ashdown normally; it is a pseudonym.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I am not going to call you by your nickname right away. Please remain standing. If you read your declaration, which will be given to you by the usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated. Mr. Ashdown, you have agreed to testify at the request of the Prosecution as part of the trial before the International Criminal Tribunal for the Former Yugoslavia against General Blaskic, who is in this courtroom. The Prosecutor has given us a summary of the main points of your testimony. You are very well familiar with the type of procedures that are in effect at this Tribunal, which to a large extent come from proceedings which you are familiar with, so you will not be surprised that you will be asked to answer the Prosecutor's questions. However, the Tribunal would very much like this testimony to be as spontaneous as possible, and that of course the Prosecutor can ask you for clarifications about this or that point. This is the scope and context, and I suppose that the Prosecutor will want to ask you a few questions first. Examination by MR. HARMON.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good afternoon, Mr. Ashdown?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Ashdown, could you first of all begin by telling the judges about your background?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was educated -- I am an Irishman by birth. I was educated in the UK at what is known as a public school, in fact a private school. I finished my education at 18. I joined the Royal Marines as an officer. I served in commando units and in the special boat section, which was the waterborne equivalent of the Special Air Service over a period of 13 years, started off at a lieutenant and ending as a captain. I saw active service in the Far East in the Borneo campaign in the early 1960s, in the Middle East in Aden, and in my own home town of Belfast in Northern Ireland. During that period I studied Chinese and took the equivalent to the first-class degree in Chinese and so left and joined the Foreign Office in 1972, and was posted as a First Secretary to the United Kingdom Permanent Mission to the United Nations in Geneva in 1974. I stayed there until 1976, when I resigned from the Foreign Service and went into politics. After a period of eight years seeking to get elected and working in local industry in my community, I was elected in 1983 to Parliament, representing the constituency of Yeovil in the south-west of England. I was then elected, in due course, Leader of my Party in 1988 and appointed a Privy Councillor to Her Majesty the Queen in 1989 and have served as both Member of Parliament for Yeovil and the Leader of my Party, the Liberal Democrats, for the last 10 years.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ashdown. Could you tell the judges if, as a member of Parliament, you took an interest in the affairs of the Former Yugoslavia and whether you visited the Former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not, Mr. Harmon -- I began to take an interest in, I suspect, July or early August 1992 when this began to be a major crisis which was appearing in British newspapers and indeed elsewhere as well. Between 1992 and the end of the conflict, I paid, in all, 10 visits.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Excuse me, if you could speak a little bit more slowly, so that the interpreters would have less trouble following you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Between 1992 and the end of the Bosnian conflict, I paid, in all, 10 visits to Bosnia, particularly to Sarajevo, during the siege, my first visit being in August 1992, my second visit being shortly afterwards, when I was invited to go to Bosnia by the Serbs, by Dr Karadzic, and at that stage I travelled throughout the Serb -- what is now known as Republika Srpska from Sarajevo through the Posavina corridor through to Banja Luka. At that time I was the first person to go into the Manjaca camp, despite some threats we received at the time from Serbs that we would be shot if we did so and, on the following day, visited Prijedor, Trnopolje. Over the subsequent eight visits, culminating in a visit right at the end of the conflict when the battle of Igman was going on, I paid in all 10 visits there, usually one during the summer and one during the winter. In December 1992, I visited the Vitez area and saw a good deal of what was going on there at that time and passed through Kiseljak, Visoko, Busovaca and Vitez, so, all in all, I paid 10 visits there. I have subsequently been back once to assist in the elections.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: On 6 May 1995, did you have a conversation with Franjo Tudjman?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did, Mr. Harmon. I was invited to attend the VE day celebrations in the Guildhall in London on 6th May 1995. It was a very large gathering -- I suppose there were of the order of 300 or 400 people there, including many Heads of State, and I was placed, presumably by somebody in the Foreign Office, because they thought I knew something about Yugoslavia, next door to President Tudjman at that time and I had an extensive conversation with him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you relate that conversation to the judges, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I made a diary note of it at the time -- it was made that night. I keep a regular diary, and, if I may, I would like to rely rather on that, but I sat next door to Mr. Tudjman. It would be fair, I think, to say that a good deal of wine was flowing at the time, and President Tudjman consumed a certain amount of that. I entered pretty swiftly into a conversation with him, and I asked him fairly early in the conversation how he believed ex Yugoslavia might look in 10 years' time, and I drew for him, on the back of the menu, which I have here, some brief lines, asking him to fill in the rest of the map as to what he believed it would look like. As I recall, I drew the --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me interrupt you right there. I will show you a copy of the map that you are referring to. With the assistance of the usher, if I could have Prosecutor's exhibit 275A and 275B placed next to the witness, Mr. Usher, if you could place, first, Prosecutor's exhibit, the 75A, on the ELMO. (Handed).

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Does the Defence have this, Mr. Harmon?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I was going to explain this is a copy of an original document. Mr. Ashdown has the originals of both documents in front of him and, prior to the commencement of these proceedings, counsel for the Defence had the opportunity to inspect the original documents. I would request, Mr. President, that the originals be kept by Mr. Ashdown and that these copies, which Mr. Ashdown will authenticate as genuine and true copies, be entered into the record. The originals will be available for the Defence at any time for further inspection. I can explain, Mr. President, that 275A, and I will pre-empt the witness a little bit, is the first diagram about which Mr. Ashdown will testify. This is a menu card on which is drawn a map, to which Mr. Ashdown contributed some of the lines and Mr. Tudjman contributed others. 275B is a copy of 275A done by Mr. Ashdown and subsequently annotated by him on the following day. But, with that having been said, Mr. President, I believe 275A is placed on the ELMO, and, please, in continuing your narrative form of testimony, Mr. Ashdown, about your conversation with President Tudjman, could you, first of all, identify this document, what it is, and what lines you particularly drew on it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, this document, Mr. Harmon, is of course the menu card for the dinner that night, and the back of it is the area which was, as you rightly say, drawn in a combination between myself and President Tudjman. I drew in this line here (indicates) which is the line of the coastline, and I marked in Sarajevo here (indicates), Belgrade there (indicates), Banja Luka here (indicates) and I put a dot over here for -- I beg your pardon, Zagreb over here and Belgrade over here -- Zagreb where the cross is and Belgrade with the dot. I put those in and said: draw for me how you see the future picture of ex-Yugoslavia. The rest of the lines on the map, including the two arrows, are those of President Tudjman's. He drew, first of all, this as the shape of Bosnia, that is, the Bosnian part of Bosnia-Herzegovina. He then drew this line here (indicates) which was the current front-line running, as it were, to the east of Banja Luka, and then he drew this line here (indicates), which is the key determining line. He said this was the division, as he saw it ending up -- incidentally, taking in Sarajevo to the west, including Banja Luka in the area belonging to the Serbs and indicating that Tuzla -- I asked him about Tuzla -- and that Tuzla would be in Serb territory -- that would be the division as it would then appear. I asked him then what was this side? He drew the arrow and said that side is Serbia and this side with this arrow drawn is Croatia. I asked him what about the Muslim area and he said, "There will be no Muslim area, except as a small element of the Croat State." I asked him, in particular, did he really expect that the Serbs would give up Banja Luka and that they would accept in exchange Tuzla, which is a predominantly Muslim community. He said yes, that is what he saw the outcome of the situation being. He then went on to say that it was his intention at or around the time that the UN mandate ended, to recapture Knin and the Krajina area around Knin. We had a discussion about this and I said: from a military point of view -- and I think I can judge these things reasonably well -- I believed that would be an exceedingly difficult military operation. This is very good defensive territory. We had a discussion as to how difficult that operation would be. He told me he believed he could do it in eight days at a loss of no more than 1,000 on his side. I recall betting him a bottle of Croat white wine to say it would take him longer and cost him more. We then went on to talk about his relations with the other two leaders, that is, Mr. Izetbegovic on the one hand and President Milosevic on the other. He was very dismissive of President Izetbegovic, who he regarded as "a fundamentalist and an Algerian" were his words. I have it in my diary he used the word "wog" as well but he found it much easier to do business with President Milosevic. He said President Milosevic was, in his words, one of us whereas President Izetbegovic was not, and I recall him saying that the Muslims were, after all, only Serbs and Croats who could not stand up to the Turks during the days of the Ottoman empire. I found this a truly extraordinary conversation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you turn to 275B and can you just place that on the ELMO and tell the judges --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I returned home that night, dictated my diary as I always do, and discussed this with my wife and said what an extraordinary conversation I had had, and,, in order to make sense of this map, the following morning I had a photocopy made, and the rest of the annotations on here are annotations of mine. In order to make it clearer for me and my records, I have actually marked in the names so: this is the Dalmatian coastline, this is Zagreb, this is the spot where Belgrade was marked. I have marked in Serbia -- all the annotations, all the writing on the map is mine -- in order to make it clearer and easier for me to understand I also marked the Xs around here which was the line President Tudjman drew indicating the current State of Bosnia. I thickened this S line, because that was the key line. I only in fact thickened it to there (indicates). That was a continuation of the line that he drew here. I did not thicken it that far.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Ashdown. I have no additional questions. Mr. President, with the court's permission, I would move into evidence, Prosecutor's exhibits 275A and B.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: No objection to 275A. I would ask that 275B be held in reserve until I conclude my cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Hayman. I do not know quite why you want us to wait. Are your questions going to determine the relevance? This is a question of identification at this point. I do not really know why this would not be entered into the record as an exhibit. The witness not only recognised it -- he is the source.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: The question is, are there portions of it that are inaccurate. For example, the top of the document states "Lines drawn by FT". The witness has testified certain of the lines on the document were drawn by him. I think we need to clarify exactly what it is. It may well be we have no objection to the document, but I cannot state that I have no objection yet until I have had a chance to question the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Let me consult with my colleagues for a moment. (Pause).

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: The judges agree that this document should be tendered as an exhibit and you can now contest it as you like. Please begin your cross-examination. Cross-examined by Mr. Hayman

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Ashdown.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you seated across from Dr Tudjman or next to him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Alongside him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who else were seated adjacent to either one of you, or rather both of you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I recall that the Croat ambassador was there or thereabouts, but I am afraid I cannot recall his position precisely.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember who was across the table from you, or was it a very wide table?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was not a very wide table as I recall. It was a standard-wide dining table. This is four years ago. I am reluctant as you will understand to extend my memory further than my diary notes, but I cannot recall who was opposite me -- if I recall, they were other Croats, but I cannot be certain of that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did anyone else besides yourself and Dr Tudjman participate in this conversation you have related?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not this conversation, as I recall, but, again, my memory, if you will forgive me beyond the bits that are on my notes is -- it is four years ago -- a little hazy, but beyond what is in my notes, I do not recall anybody else participating in this conversation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell the Trial Chamber how long this exchange lasted -- the exchange you have related involving the creation of the map; the drawing on the menu is what I am referring to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. Hayman, that is really very difficult. It was a long dinner, there were speeches. Clearly, we talked about other matters as well. I mean, you know, small talk, and I must have talked to the person on my other side, but I would have said that this portion, that is the interesting portion of the conversation contained in the diary notes, would have been of the order of 20 minutes, perhaps half an hour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in what language did the two of you converse?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: English.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you speak Serbo-Croat?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ask Dr Tudjman to draw a map relating to Bosnia, or relating to the Former Yugoslavia as a whole?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I asked him to draw -- to tell me how he believed the situation in the Former Yugoslavia, particularly of course pertaining to -- since that was the issue at the time, to the Bosnia and Herzegovina area, but it was about the area of Former Yugoslavia in this region.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could exhibit 275A be placed and illuminated on the ELMO, please? You indicated that you drew certain items on this map --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- to initiate the exchange, if you will; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, do you see within the upper left-hand quadrant, if you will, of the circle, that you have described as, to your belief, constituting Bosnia and Herzegovina, do you see that there appears to be an X, a small B and a box?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us first of all -- did you draw any of those three markings?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I drew, as I said in my diary notes -- I put a cross for Zagreb. I drew these lines, I drew the coastline, I put a cross for Zagreb, a cross for Banja Luka and a cross for Sarajevo and, if I recall, a dot for Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where is the dot?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The dot will be under the cross, that is here (indicates) on the map -- I annotated the map the following day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it on exhibit 275A, the dot?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Let me have a look. No, I do not see -- well -- I suspect it is this point here, but I cannot be certain (indicates).

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I am sorry, you are referring to the original?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am referring --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you could place the original on the ELMO, then we can follow. Do you see on the original banquet menu the dot, which you have related as indicating Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. Hayman, of course we are not dealing here with a precise piece of cartography, as you will understand, but there is in the middle of the crease of the menu at the point of the arrow a dot, and I think if you look at this, you will be able to see it. It is just about there at the point of the arrow (indicates) I suspect -- I would have placed my pen there and said: let us assume Belgrade is there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you place -- I do not know if the ELMO will hold both these documents, but could you put exhibit 275B next to the original menu map so hopefully we can see as much as possible -- that is fine -- thank you to the technical booth. Can you indicate on 275B where Belgrade is marked?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is marked there (indicates).

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you agree that is a bit of a distance from the crease on the original banquet menu?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Hayman, I would be happy to agree that. Remember, that I was drawing a map from a conversation the following day. Inevitably, this was not intended as a map that would be subject to detailed cross-examination in a court like this. If you look on the original of the photocopy the following day, you can quite clearly see that the Belgrade that I have marked, unlike the other crosses -- the other crosses are in black but the Belgrade is in my ink of the following day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I take it, though, that Belgrade was denoted with a circle in the course of the banquet dinner?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Belgrade was not denoted with a circle. I recall if I remember putting -- I recall drawing the -- it is very difficult four years later, but I recall drawing the left-hand crosses and saying: let us assume that Belgrade is there, and resting my pen. It did not seem to me that the position of Belgrade, which presumably would be reasonably well known and far away from the conflict, was something that was of great importance. The importance of this was Sarajevo and Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it fair to say the next morning you improved the map by putting Belgrade in a location where you thought it should be in relation to the other elements of the map?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I did not improve the map. I annotated the map in order that I had a decent recollection of the conversation as it took place -- I believed that to be accurate.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So is it your testimony that you did or did not mark in a visible manner with a pen at the banquet the location of Belgrade, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I marked it by putting my pen on the menu card and leaving behind as I recall a dot, and, when I, in some hurry, and I suppose quite roughly the following morning, made annotations, I may well have put Belgrade in a different place --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: The Tribunal is sufficiently informed on this point, Mr. Hayman. Move on, please. I believe that the witness has already answered.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I think he has, Mr. President. I do not have another question about where Belgrade came from on exhibit 275B.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you could direct your attention to 275A, Mr. Ashdown, and perhaps we could focus in on that document and remove 275B for the moment so that it can be seen more clearly. Next to the cross, which you have said indicates Banja Luka, do you see a small B?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you recall who made that notation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: To indicate?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: To indicate it was Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The small box next to the B, did you make that notation as well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I really cannot remember, Mr. Hayman, who made that notation. You must forgive me. I do not think the box has any significance. We were discussing things at dinner with plates being moved around, dishes being served, glasses of wine being filled. It may well be a pen inadvertently on this very historical document made a mark it should not have done. I really cannot remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was it a very relaxed setting at the dinner?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, it was a formal state dinner in many ways.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Dr Tudjman enjoy the hospitality being shown to him at the dinner?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And he enjoyed the wine?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you enjoy the wine as well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did enjoy the wine.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you say he became perhaps somewhat intoxicated in the course of the evening?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If I am blunt with you, I can remember saying that -- I can remember finding the conversation so fascinating that he -- his wine glass appeared to be full for a good deal of the time, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you agree that he appeared to become somewhat intoxicated in the course of the banquet?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. Hayman, he is a Head of State. I do not want to use words which would be insulting. Suffice it to say I think he enjoyed himself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you, did you feel somewhat the effects of the wine in the course of the banquet?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I enjoyed myself as well, Mr. Hayman. However, I am --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Gentlemen, gentlemen, let me bring us back to serenity in these proceedings. I did not think that we would make inferences about the state of inebriation of a Head of State in this courtroom. This was an official banquet, and there was excellent wine there. Please move to the next question.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: If you could direct your attention to 275B, please. At the top someone has written "Lines drawn by Franjo Tudjman"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is me -- I drew those -- I made those two annotations at the top.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. I take it you do not mean to suggest that you drew the far -- the line to the far lower left-hand corner?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Excuse me?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You do not mean to suggest that Dr. Tudjman drew that line. You drew that line?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As my diary records at the time, I drew that line. The other lines there -- as far as I was concerned when I made that annotation, the interesting lines on this map were drawn by Franjo Tudjman and not by me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You see these large lines, one coming from Banja Luka in the upper left-hand corner. If you go all the way up the upper left-hand corner and find in Banja Luka in Croatia, you see there is a line dropping down from that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is an arrow.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So that is not a line?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, it is an indicator. If you have a look and see what -- I have done the annotations with an arrow to indicate what they are indicating.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All the arrows were not lines and they were not drawn by Dr. Tudjman, they were drawn by you; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: With respect to the S and the division, did Dr. Tudjman in your discussions say that there would be a Croat Federation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. You will see that he drew very clearly the two arrows, and I said, "What is this side?" He drew an arrow and said: that is Serbia. I said: and what is this side. He drew an arrow and he said: that is Croatia. He said that the Muslim State, Bosnian State, would not exist; it would be an insignificant part, as I recall -- my diary notes -- an insignificant part of the Croat Federation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Of the Croat Federation. What did you understand that to be referring to, the Croat Federation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I meant that it would be -- what would be essentially Croatia with a dominant Croatia in control.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Not part of the Republic of Croatia, but some element of territory in some Federal or federation relationship with Croatia, perhaps?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The words in my diary are the ones that I would wish to fall back on here, because they are exactly what he said as I recall them. He said they would be an insignificant part of the Croat Federation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My focus is on "Croat Federation" and whether he told you that the Croat Federation would be in federation with Croatia, or in federation with other component parts of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I got it absolutely clearly that it would be in federation with Croatia. As far as I was concerned, this was going to be -- the impression I got was this would be Greater Croatia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he say that to you -- that was your impression. Did he say that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, he did not say that, Mr. Hayman, as I recall, but I think the arrow and the indication shows perfectly clearly that he sees two elements here, a Serb element and a Croat element, and that Croat element would be of a single unitary nature and it would be with Croatia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he refer to those elements as cultural in nature, or as constituting a State, one State on each side of the S, or did he not specify, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He only referred to it -- I mean cultural I suppose, Mr. Hayman, and I am trying -- this is a dinner-table conversation -- the only indication that I would have had that he saw that as being cultural, was that there was a very strong racist overtone in his approach to Muslims, and I think he regarded the Muslim element as an inferior element, who basically did not matter in the outcome; they were going to be part of Croatia. The only cultural element I can think of was in his very insulting, almost racist approach, to Muslims.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But I take it he did not specify beyond that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Whether he was referring to Croat territory as culturally Croat, or being inhabited by ethnic Croats versus part of the Croat State, that is, the Republic of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, the significant point was that he said that he regarded the Muslims as having a very small part to play and of no significance and this was a matter between himself and President Milosevic. This was going to be settled as between Croatia and Serbia and I got the firm view, in the conversation, that this was an already done deal, that this was an agreement. I mean, we all, of course, know that there is some suspicion about such a deal being in existence and the famous Tito Hunting Lodge Agreement. The clear indication I got was the result of the offensive that would be launched at or around August or September of that year would be in settlement of the outstanding Bosnian/Muslim problem and that settlement would be a division between Croatia on the one hand and Serbia on the other. I can draw no other conclusion but that conclusion from the two arrows that are drawn on the map and indeed from his conversation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, he told you, did he not, that he would launch a military action to retake the Krajina in the late summer or fall of 1995; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As I recall, he linked this to the end of the UN mandate, and of course, at that time, the UN mandate would have been known to end around about the end of the summer -- at all events, the following morning when I got my diary notes back -- and I always ask for my diary notes back -- they are typed by my secretary -- I entered into the diary that he told me that, quite bluntly, at the end of the UN mandate, they would then take the Knin/Krajina probably in August or September. When that subsequently happened, I felt it was right and proper to make sure this conversation and this map was released into the public domain, because I wanted the international community to know what I believed his intentions were, how they had been pre-planned. I believe it is fair to say, by so doing, we may well have limited the achievement of those ambitions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: To return to my question for a moment, he told you then that he intended, when the UN mandate expired in the Krajina, to retake the Krajina by force with the Croat military -- correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was the indication.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In fact, that subject was the subject of a wager between the two of you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he tell you, at any time during the dinner, that he planned to undertake a military action to take any part of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, he did not say that, but it must be perfectly clear from the map that he drew, because the clear implication was that the Krajina operation was the first stage of an operation to bring about the situation which he described when he drew the map.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That was the inference you drew; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was the inference I drew. My own military experience tells me that, when you start these things, it is best to continue, especially if you are on the kind of roll he thought he was going to be on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it your testimony that, when you left the banquet, you believed some kind of agreement between Tudjman and Milosevic was in place -- was that your belief at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was never discussed, but it was my belief that this was the fulfilment of an understanding as between President Tudjman and President Milosevic. I concluded that, if he was serious about retaking the Krajina, then it would have been impossible for him to do so, militarily, without extraordinary loss of life and huge military campaigns, unless there had been a tacit understanding about the release of the Knin Krajina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you stating you believe there was a deal regarding the Krajina or a deal involving Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The deal is the map. The deal is the S on the map -- that is the deal.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you believe that that deal existed when you left the banquet?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I left -- I left believing that such a deal was likely to be in existence. I have no proof of it but I left believing that that was a strong probability.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you got your typed notes back fairly shortly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I mean, forgive me, I cannot remember exactly how long, but the normal routine is I will dictate my diary on the night. Very, very occasionally I will do it the following night but within usually a few hours -- I dictate them at the end of the day, they are given to my secretary, they are typed up. I would have had these back within I suppose six days, something like that. That would be the normal --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you got the notes back, and you of course had your map, did you believe you were in possession of information potentially of diplomatic or intelligence significance?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I could not believe that it was likely that what President Tudjman said he was going to do he would actually do. I had a document which I regarded as being of historical information, but I would not go further than that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you agree that, at the time, in June of 1995, it was a matter of public record that President Tudjman and the Republic of Croatia took the position that, unless there was a political agreement by autumn, Croatia would launch a military campaign to recover the occupied areas of Croatia, where rebels had proclaimed a breakaway republic of the Serb Krajina -- would you agree that was a matter of public record at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. Hayman, forgive me, I cannot either agree or disagree to that. I do not recall such a matter being in the public record at the time. You must forgive me. My recollection -- my recall of what happened in June and precise chronology beyond that is not something I can comment on here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you think the information you had received regarding a military intention to launch an action in the Krajina was something confidential, or information that was not in the public domain at the time you received it in June 1995?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, received it in May, but --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Excuse me, yes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not believe the information he gave me was in the public domain, no. I certainly did not believe that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I take it, in May, you did not release the map or grant any interviews?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What caused you to change your mind and release this information to the news media?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As I believe I have already said, it was the fulfilment of what President Tudjman had told me, and the Serb assault on the Krajina in, I think I am right in saying, 6th or 7th August of that year, and as I watched that unfold, and I watched indeed the Croat troops taking Knin, which is something I thought they could not do without huge loss, I became very concerned indeed that what I was seeing was the de facto partitioning of this area between Croatia and Serbia and I believed it therefore right that I should place the information that I had in the public domain, because I believed that would be one way of alerting the international community about what President Tudjman's intentions were, and I think it is fair to say, given the reaction to that, that it may well be that certain members of the international community were alerted to his ambitions as a result of that, and that they were not therefore fulfilled.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I take it the Croat military did not enter Bosnia Herzegovina as a part of Operation Storm -- is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am sorry, Mr. Hayman, I really cannot comment on that. I do not know whether they entered Bosnia-Herzegovina or not at that stage.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you have any information suggesting that they did?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: None at all, but I do not have any information suggesting they do not. I am not an expert on exactly how far they got on that operation. Well, I can --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you granted these interviews in August of 1995, how many interviews did you grant?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, as I recall, I considered the best way to try and release this, and I believed it was best to try and release it as an exclusive to The Times newspaper, and I suppose that parlance is "leaked" it to The Times newspaper, as a result of which I was asked to do some interviews, and I did them. I really cannot recall how many. I do not think they were -- I can do 8 or 10 interviews a day quite often if the story is a big one. I do not think there were as many as that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In one of those interviews, were you asked, if you believed there was a secret deal between Croatia and Serbia with the ultimate aim of carving up Bosnia and did you reply, "I do not know. All I do know is that what President Tudjman told me at that dinner has proved to be accurate so far"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I really cannot remember how I responded to every question that was asked. It would not, however, be unreasonable -- I mean, if I am to make a public statement about a private suspicion, you can sometimes get yourself into a position where you have to justify that in very precise and very detailed terms. It is one thing to have a private suspicion about something. It is another to voice that private suspicion in a very public way. So, it could be that I answered in those terms. It would not in any way diminish the strength of my private suspicion about such a deal being in existence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you agree with the statement, "I do not think the map should be seen as a plan or an intention. Maybe it is only a prediction" -- do you agree with that statement with respect to the map from the dinner?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When this map was drawn, I saw this as a prediction, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And even in August of 1995, after Operation Storm had been launched, would you still have agreed with the statement that the map should not be seen as a plan or an intention?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think it is perfectly possible for this to have been a prediction of a further operation beyond Operation Storm, so I do not have any difficulty about that statement. Operation Storm may well have been one which was confined for instance to the Krajina, but I certainly believed if that was going to succeed that was at least the first element of something that may have gone further.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If an article, Mr. President, could be provided to the witness, there is a French translation of it as well for the record -- this is a Press Association news file story dated 7 August 1995, headlined "I Saw Bosnia Carve-up Map says Ashdown". (Handed). It is fairly short, I think, Mr. Ashdown. We should give you a chance to read it quickly, with an emphasis on the bottom half of the one-paragraph story?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Fine.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall making statements in substance equivalent to these in the course of the interviews you gave in August of 1995?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: To be honest, Mr. Hayman, I do not recall it but I have no reason to believe it inaccurate.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you agree with the statements attributed to you herein?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have no reason to believe the statement is inaccurate.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As you sit here today?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Absolutely. Nor is it inconsistent, it seems to me, with what I believed was then under way. I wanted people to know. One of the purposes as I quite clearly say here is to ensure that the Krajina operation, if it were to go further -- and I had reason to believe it might have done -- if it were to go further was to make sure it did not step into Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that was your purpose?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My purpose --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Excuse me -- that was your purpose in leaking the map, providing the map, and granting interviews; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. Hayman, my purpose was to alert the international community to what I believed were the intentions, long or short term, of President Tudjman based on the information he gave me at that dinner and on the map.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Again, if exhibit 275B could be placed on the ELMO, it may still be up there. If so, if the ELMO could be activated. B is the map including annotations. I take it that it was your understanding from this map that everything to the right of the S would be ceded to Serbia as part of an agreement between Croatia and Serbia; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. Hayman, I can go no further than the words I have used to you. I can only tell you that President Tudjman drew the S along with the other lines I have talked about. I concluded from the conversation that he regarded everything to the left of that map as Greater Croatia, and everything to the right of that map, as, as it were, Greater Serbia. My private suspicion, strong private suspicion, at the time was that that conversation and this map indicated -- I will not go any further -- that there was a possibility of an agreement between them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Directing your attention to 275B, is there a portion to the north, if you will, or to the upper part of the page, from the boundary of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Here (indicates)?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, namely Territory of the Republic of Croatia, that is within the right-hand portion of the S?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You must forgive me, Mr. Hayman, I am not yet terribly clear exactly what your question is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In other words, above, if you will, the barbed wire line?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But below and to the right of the heavy S, the top of the S, there is a slice of territory; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You mean in this area here (indicates)?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And your understanding of the map is that that territory would constitute part of Greater Serbia; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I mean I will tell you how I believe it to be. Do please remember this is not an Ordnance Survey map; this is a map written at a dinner. As I recall it, I would have seen this as being the line of the Savja River here, and the area between the Savja River and the barbed wire as being the Posavina corridor, with Brcko about here. It does not actually match up with the map, because we all know perfectly well that the Savja River is the line of the Bosnian border and the barbed wire is the line of the Bosnian border. This was a minor inaccuracy in what I think is the main point of this map, which is the line of the S drawn in relation to Greater Serbia and Greater Croatia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ask Dr. Tudjman about that piece of territory?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. The important point was not have we got this cartographically absolutely perfect -- the important point was that in this map there was no place for Bosnia and a minor place for Muslims in what I regarded to be a Greater Croatia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you agree that, if the barbed wire line is the boundary of Bosnia and Herzegovina, then the territory --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: To the north of it?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: To the north of it constitutes, in part at least, the area of Western Slavonia and Eastern Slavonia, which is within the Republic of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct, I agree with that, but I do not think the map was that accurate. I took this line here of the S to be the line of the Savjo River. This was written -- drawn by a man who had had a couple or three glasses of wine, and was enjoying a good dinner, and I do not suppose that the precise position of the Savja River and the precise position of the Bosnian border was necessarily known to him. It was not an issue we discussed. The important point of this map is: how does it divide up Bosnia and what does it do to the Muslim community.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It is fair to say then the map was hastily drawn?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is perfectly fair to say. You do not have to be a brain surgeon to look at this map and to know that it was hastily drawn.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that there was no discussion concerning exactly what was what, other than the arrows you have indicated, such as the territory which appears to be Western and Eastern Slavonia on this map?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My diary notes at the time said this, "He took his pen and drew a broad S-shaped line starting in Slavonia and then running along the lines of the Savja River" -- that is why I presume this is the line of the Savja River, which is the Bosnian/Croat border, and then along the lines -- "including Tuzla and then back to the east of Sarajevo", down here, "and back to the sea", so that is what -- that is my diary note. "I drew the coast in for him, Zagreb, Belgrade, Sarajevo, then left the rest to him. He took his pen and drew a broad S-shaped line starting in Slavonia" up here "and running along the lines of the Savja River" which is the Bosnia Croat border "including Tuzla", so Tuzla was here, "including Tuzla, east of Sarajevo, and then down to the sea". I think that is pretty clear.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At the time, did the Serbs hold Slavonia, that is, they held that portion of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Serbs, at the time, if I recall held West Slavonia -- I beg your pardon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Vukovar, did they hold Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If I recall -- forgive me, I cannot remember at that time what the Serbs held and what they did not hold.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So at least, with respect to the top of the S, the map more accurately reflects what land was then held by the Serbs -- it accurately reflected that with respect to territories within the Republic of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am sorry, I do not understand -- I do not understand your question, Mr. Hayman.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I will ask another one.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Let me see if I can clarify absolutely. I took this to be (indicates) the Savja River, this point here. I took this area here, the line between the barbed wire, as you put it, and the Savja River was what you and I both know is the Posavina corridor, with Brcko at one side and that seemed to be a reflection of what was the position on the ground.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: With respect to the northern part of the boundary, which is marked as "Present Bosnia-Herzegovina border" --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, if you are asking me: was there anything indicated in our conversation that there was a deal for the Krajina on the one hand and Eastern Slavonia on the other, I do not believe anything in our conversation indicated that deal.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In fact, you would agree it would be preposterous to suggest that Croatia would deal away --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I do not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- Eastern Slavonia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You must forgive me, I do not agree with that at all. We all know that that is reported to be the current Karadordevo exchange. I know that and you know that. All I can tell you is the bit we were talking about at the time was perfectly consistent with, as it were, the Bosnian element of what is reported to be the Hunting Lodge Agreement. And, you know, if it is the case that, for instance, Serbia at that stage was prepared -- I grant you that is contentious -- to give up the Knin and the Krajina -- and, looking at the military operation, one has to conclude they did not fight very hard for it at the time -- then it seems to be perfectly possible that there could have been an exchange along the lines you suggest.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And this map would dictate such an exchange; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I do not go any further than this map showed me what he told me that night in respect of Bosnia and the division of Bosnia. We did not talk about Eastern Slavonia at the time as I recall it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You would agree we know as we sit here today that Eastern Slavonia was not ceded to Serbia as part of any deal or agreement; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Whether you know that, or whether you do not, there are those who have a view that it may well have been part of the plan. But all I can tell you is what this map tells me about what happened that night, and it is exclusively concentrated on the area of Bosnia, and in particular the positions of the Muslims.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you agree that Eastern Slavonia is part of Croatia today?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I would object to additional questions about Eastern Slavonia. The witness has testified repeatedly what this map represents and what his understanding of the map is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I think that is a valid objection, Mr. Hayman. You are emphasising a great deal on that point even though the witness is telling you what he saw, what he talked about, about the map. I think he said it already.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Did you write in your notes, the evening of the dinner, that it was clear to you what the game plan was? "He", presumably referring to Dr. Tudjman, "will try and come to some kind of an agreement with the Serbs as soon as they have taken militarily as much as they can from each other."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know where you are quoting on that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This is the second line of the last full paragraph.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is perfectly clear -- yes, fine, that was my recollection at the time, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In other words, that there was no agreement, but that you thought there might be an intention to reach an agreement after the Croats and the Serbs had battled to a standstill; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that the line he drew was a line which he believed would produce -- whether by agreement or not -- an acceptable position for both sides, that is, Croatia -- Greater Croatia on the one hand and Greater Serbia on the other, which would allow them adequately and with satisfaction on both sides to divide up the territory of Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you came away from the dinner, Mr. Ashdown, believing that there was no such agreement in existence at that time; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I came away from the dinner exactly as I have said, strongly suspecting that such an agreement could well be in existence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But that is not what you dictated in your notes that night; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is not what I have dictated here, but that is what I believed at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Since the dinner, after you made your annotations, did you send a copy of the map to Dr. Tudjman -- has he seen it again?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you talked to him since?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you take an intense disliking to Dr. Tudjman in the course of the dinner?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot say I find him a very pleasant man, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that is how you felt at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is how I felt at the time. Yes, that is how I felt at the time, and -- yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If the usher could assist, Mr. President. This is an English language news article consisting of two pages, if it could be provided to the witness, dated 10th June 1995, The Financial Times, London, headline "Croat Threat of New War Against Serbs". It is two pages -- there should be a second page. You have two pages front and back on your copies: if I could direct your attention to the third and fourth paragraphs from the bottom of the first page beginning: "In Croatia, rebel Serb aircraft..." I will read it so we can have a sight translation; my apologies to the translating booths: "In Croatia rebel Serb aircraft --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Tell us the context of this article.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: This was about five weeks after the dinner, prior to the witness's decision in August to share his experience, his encounter with the news media, so it is during the intervening time period.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Reading the third and fourth paragraphs from the bottom: "In Croatia, rebel Serb aircraft bombed Croat positions, and President Franjo Tudjman threatened to recover control of all Serb-controlled areas of his republic by force. He said that unless there was a political agreement by autumn, he would launch a military campaign to recover the occupied areas of Croatia, where rebels have proclaimed a breakaway `republic of the Serb Krajina'." My question for you, Mr. Ashdown, is: with respect to Dr. Tudjman's comments of a political offensive in the Krajina, are they in substance the same as those related in the paragraphs I have read?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You are asking me for an opinion, Mr. Hayman. You know, I really am not able -- I am able to give you the conversation I had with him and the conclusions I reached. I am really not able -- you must forgive me -- I do not regard myself to be an expert of this period and what went on there -- to give an opinion about a Financial Times article published a month later which I have not seen until now. Whether or not this represents an accurate report, for instance, of what happened at the time, or accurate intentions, I really cannot, I am afraid, comment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your decision to release the map, share it, whatever, was motivated by your concerns at the time of Operation Storm. Do you recall whether at the same time you were receiving information that a military build-up around Eastern Slavonia was occurring with respect to some approximately 150 Serb tanks as well as Croat military elements?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Forgive me, Mr. Hayman, I just cannot recall such information. There were reports and counter-reports and lots of them all over that period. It may or may not have been the case that I noted such information but I cannot recall whether I did or not. What I saw was -- what I saw was, it seemed to me, a prediction made by President Tudjman now coming true before my eyes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I am going to object to this line of questioning. The questioning which was taken by the Prosecutor on direct examination was very focused, particularly about a dinner conversation. We are now going into the military history of various campaigns in the Former Yugoslavia, and I would object.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: The issue, Mr. President --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Hayman, I sustain the objection. This witness was called by the Prosecution to speak about what happened at a banquet on 6th May 1995. He said everything that he knows about the dinner. If you are asking questions to see to what extent the information he is bringing about that conversation might relate to the proceedings relating to the Defence and Croatia's position, that is something that the judges do understand, but we cannot get into a Chief of Staff conference in order to know whether he could know this or he could know that. This is somebody who was at a banquet, with Mr. Tudjman. Perhaps you could move to another question. Having said this, you have shown a document. I would like us to complete the questioning about that document, but quickly, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I will withdraw the document, but I would ask, if I am not allowed to go beyond matters of fact, then expert opinions and political opinions and military opinions that the witness has given should be stricken, because he was not a fact witness; he did not limit himself to matters of fact that he personally experienced. That is the reason that we find it necessary to ask him about, for example, the logic or lack of logic of a deal involving Eastern Slavonia, which I have left.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: With all the respect that I have for the Defence's position, Mr. Hayman, I do not quite agree with you. In this trial, like in all trials, there is a witness who is called by one of the parties -- called on a very specific point, Mr. Harmon, and that is why we ask for a resume before the witness comes in. The summary was very clear. The cross-examination must be limited to the main points of the examination-in-chief. It is natural for you to try to show to what extent the credibility of the opinion expressed by the witness can be tested and you must recognise that the judges have shown a great deal of latitude on this point. Please, complete what you have to ask about that point. I am not trying to stop you from asking questions, but you have to understand that we have been dealing with this political issue for a long time -- whether this is fiction or not, but we cannot say that this person played an active role in the politics of that area. If you could please finish quickly and then move to another question, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: If I may have a moment, Mr. President. (Pause). Mr. President, there are a few items that I think should be covered in closed session -- sensitive items which the witness has said are sensitive, and we respect that, and, beyond that and offering I believe one or two articles that I have tendered, I have no further questions in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. President, I have one question on redirect examination. Re-examination by MR. HARMON.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: If you would refer to your diary note, Mr. Hayman he read a certain portion of a sentence starting on the second paragraph from the bottom second line. Mr. Hayman read the following portion to you: "He will try to come to some kind of agreement with the Serbs as soon as they have taken militarily as much as they can from each other." Can you read the remainder of that sentence, the rest of that sentence that Mr. Hayman did not read?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: "Then they will both turn on the Muslims and wipe them out."

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you, I have no additional questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I would like to ask your opinion, Mr. Harmon, about the issue of the private session. As far as I am concerned, I thought that we had completed this testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: It is hard for me to comment on points that the Defence counsel wishes to raise with the Chamber. I thought we had concluded as well but I think counsel, if he has some points that he needs to raise with the Chamber, should raise those points and perhaps if they are sensitive enough, they should be raised in closed session.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I can do so in private session, Mr. President. I do not think there is any need to lower the blinds. I think it will be brief. (Pause)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: The Trial Chamber has agreed to a private session for the few questions which have to supplement the cross-examination. Mr. Registrar, could have we have a private session arranged, but quickly, Mr. Hayman. (Private session)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: (Open session)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I think that the examination-in-chief and cross-examination are now completed. I would like to turn to my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Ashdown?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You had this opportunity of having an uninhibited dialogue with Dr. Tudjman, and perhaps the flow of wine made it vino veritas. Perhaps you can help me understand more of the concrete implication of some of the statements, and of the map. Could you agree that this map is just an indication that Bosnia should not exist any more?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe that is what he meant. I am sure President Tudjman is extremely used to banquets and indeed I am. Alcohol is not unknown in these matters. I still believe that he was reflecting perfectly accurately, perfectly sanely, and perfectly logically what his intentions were and what he believed was the answer that he felt most accurate to the question that I put to him, which is: how do you see Bosnia-Herzegovina in 10 years' time, and his answer was, basically, it will not exist.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Cut it into half and each one -- Serbia and Croatia will annex what they have won?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That, sir, is the clear implication of the map and the conclusion that I reached that night, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, did he in one way or another indicate what he would do with the citizens, with the Bosniaks, where will he send them, what will he do with them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, he did not. He said he believed the Muslims would be a very small and insignificant part of the Croat State, but there was no indication in what he said that he was intending genocide or anything like that. I am not saying that that would not have been actions that his subordinates might have taken, but he gave me no indications along those lines, but he certainly showed an attitude to the Muslim community, which I regarded to be -- well, it is a very strong word to use, but which I regarded to be racist.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I beg your pardon?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Which I regarded to be racist -- it is a strong word, but, I think not an inaccurate --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said he said clearly that "Milosevic is one of us"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But "Izetbegovic is not one of us"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This must not only have applied to Milosevic; it must have applied to his people, too, or Izetbegovic as a person?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not think he showed any particular love or regard for Mr. Izetbegovic as a person, but I am bound to say that his general comments seemed to me to indicate that his approach to this was one based rather more on race than individuals.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On race?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And he thought that this race does not constitute part of the nation -- they are not part of this territory?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, if I may read it to you, I think the most interesting comment was: "The Muslims are, after all, only Serbs and Croats who were too weak to stand up to the Turks and the Ottoman Empire.". I think that gives the very clear indication of the fact that he believed that Bosnia was a strange creation which ought not to have existed and really what we are talking about is Greater Serbia and Greater Croatia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
