utterances.text: He did not indicate what he would do with these foreign element?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They would be simply an insignificant part of the Croat Federation, by which I took him to mean the Greater Croat Federation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Mr. Ashdown, as you mentioned in the course of your career, you have sat at many dinner parties and you have acquired experience of people speaking in circumstances in which wine was flowing. Would I be understanding you correctly to say that, in the course of that experience, you yourself have retained your ability to judge the words spoken or things said or done, whether they represent the considered views of your interlocutor or represent the influence of alcohol?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As I am sure you are aware, both the life of a politician and the life of a diplomat revolve a good deal on having private conversations which are off the record but which are nevertheless regarded as very revealing, because they show intention. I must have done this now professionally -- by which I take my role as a diplomat and as a politician -- for 25 years now. It is usually the case that such conversations take place over dinner and sometimes over lunch. It is normally the case that alcohol will be present. It is also the case that your professional ability and standing depends on you making appropriate judgements as to whether what you have been told is the truth or not. In many previous circumstances similarly as a diplomat I will have sat next door to Heads of State, senior other diplomats, at long dinners which have included a certain consumption of alcohol and had to write telegrams home the following day, upon which my Government would have, at that time, determined foreign policy and certain aspects. This was to me an event both in terms of its nature, and in terms of its alcohol consumption, since that is a point that seems to be of some importance, and in terms of -- the nature of the private conversation is one I am well used to. I think it would be fair to say of all the private conversations I have had in these circumstances, this must rank amongst the most historically interesting, as far as I am concerned, but this is not an unusual experience for me over the last 25 or 30 years.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Should the court take it that, in the judgement which you made at the time, the lines drawn by President Tudjman and the things which he said about the likely shape of the political geography of the area in 10 years' time represented his views?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe they represented both his considered views and his hopes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I would like to ask two questions of the witness. The first has to do with the map that you drew -- I think this is a question that was already asked -- excuse me for asking it again but I want further clarification. Do you think that what was reserved for the Muslims was part of a Croat/Muslim Federation or did you think that it was really a cutting up of Bosnia, that Bosnia would no longer exist and that there would be a Greater Croatia? I believe you answered the question but, excuse me, I would like for my own sake, to form an opinion about what you said?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, I take that firm view, that what we were talking about here was a Greater Croatia, and a Greater Serbia. It was not about a Bosniak Federation as between Bosnia and Herzegovina, or the Muslims and the Croats. It was a Greater Croatia and a Greater Serbia and I believe, sir, that that is quite clearly indicated on the map by the two arrows -- the two arrows -- I do not know if I can actually use this -- the two arrows here (indicates) these are arrows which extend well beyond the borders of the Krajina into Croatia and on this side clearly beyond the borders of Bosnia, the border of Bosnia being indicated by what Mr. Hayman called the barbed wire. I took it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Are you the one who put the arrows in?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, these two arrows were drawn by President Tudjman, and it is very clear from that that in fact what he saw was a Greater Serbia and a Greater Croatia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, you were very clear. My second question has to do with the way you managed this secret or at least this diplomatic confidence. Rest assured that I am not speaking about the quantity or quality of the wine that was or was not served at that dinner, but I would like to ask why you did not speak about this to the official authorities of your country. You felt that it was very important -- I think John Major was the Prime Minister at the time -- that you did not go to speak to the Minister of Foreign Affairs. You are a politician, you know many people, you are familiar with the territory, but in the end you chose to go to the media to speak about what you were present at, whereas you yourself said it was of a significance which appeared to you to be at that time to be historical, but you did not rush to speak to the Minister of Foreign Affairs, or to John Major and say -- I do not want to say 'scoop', but "I have information which is very important." Perhaps it is a question which is not discreet and if you find it to be indiscreet, please do not answer it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. President, I apologise, but I have to give you a somewhat equivocal answer here. I seem to recollect, and please forgive me for not being able to be clear about it but I will be able to be clear after, I seem to recollect that I did consider this conversation sufficiently important to report it to the Foreign Secretary at the time. I certainly passed on to the Foreign Secretary at the time several reports that I had had from -- when I was visiting Bosnia-Herzegovina, and it was my normal practice to submit reports to the Government on a confidential basis when I returned. I seem to recollect, but I can confirm that, if you wish later, that I did pass this on, but at the time, this struck me as being such an extraordinary conversation, I found it difficult to believe that a head of State, frankly, could be so indiscreet, and the reason why subsequently -- whether or not I informed my Government, and I apologise for not being able to answer that directly -- the reason why subsequently I released this into the public domain was the reasons that I gave -- I wanted to alert the international community to what I regarded to be the long-term intentions of President Tudjman based on this conversation. I am sorry I cannot answer your first question as plainly as I would like. If the court wishes, I could certainly discover if I did that, if it is material to this and let you know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: So could I then conclude, without extrapolating your thoughts, that you did not inform the Prime Minister nor the Minister of Foreign Affairs of the United Kingdom?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, forgive me -- I am having to give an indeterminate answer here, but I seem to recollect that I did, but at this distance I cannot remember. It was certainly the case that I was passing many pieces of information back to the Government when I visited Bosnia -- I would normally do a report when I got back of a confidential nature and I seem to recollect that I passed this information on to the Foreign Secretary at the time, but I cannot be absolutely clear about that, Sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDAN
utterances.text: Any further questions?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: You just mentioned something interesting. You said that you were rather surprised that Dr. Tudjman was so indiscreet. Now, he is a public figure and accustomed as much as you are -- or more -- to talking at dinner with the flow of wine. Do you think this indiscretion was meant to convey a message to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I do not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Or was it just a little talk?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have heard it subsequently said -- forgive me, I do not wish to be rude about a head of State, but I have heard it said since that President Tudjman can be quite frank in such conversations. I was surprised. I certainly had not met him before, I certainly had not had a conversation of this nature with him before. I am absolutely certain he was speaking to me at the time about what he believed at that time was going to happen. I certainly do not believe he had any intention that this should be sent as a warning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: A last point. Have you heard anything from Mr. Tudjman since then expressing his regret that you had given out that information? Did he call you up; did he say anything to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, Sir, but I certainly have been told by the Croat Ambassador that Croatia was very displeased at the time when this map was leaked. Perhaps it would be worthwhile explaining -- I do not make a habit of putting conversations such as this in the private domain. I took my own personal decision on that. I take responsibility for that decision. Others may wish to criticise it. I believe that, at the time, it was the right thing to do, because I was very concerned that an extremely delicate situation in Bosnia-Herzegovina -- peace was just beginning to become possible -- could have been disrupted, if apart from taking the Krajina, there had been an attempt to cross over the border and complete this map on the ground. I did not take that decision lightly -- I took it after very considerable consideration. If President Tudjman believes that, you know, this may have been a confidence betrayed, I would understand that. I still believe, on balance, the decision I took very seriously at the time to put this in the public domain was the right decision. I believe that is vindicated by the fact that the Krajina operation was -- that the international community did take action to ensure that the Krajina operation did not go further and therefore disrupt the possibilities of peace in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Have you had the opportunity of going back to Zagreb?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you given a visa?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, sir. I have not -- I passed through Split shortly after the peace and went to try and help my colleagues in the Bosnian Liberals, for whom I have a huge admiration. They are very highly courageous. They are the ones who smuggled me across Igman and put me through the underground tunnel into Sarajevo during the battle of Igman in a Renault 5. I went back as an act of gratitude to help them with their election campaigning. At that stage, briefly, I passed through Croatia, but I have not been to Zagreb since.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I would like to conclude this hearing, to tell you on behalf of my colleagues, how sensitive we are to you having coming here, to have testified, in such a way -- about things which you considered very important. As a parliamentarian of a great nation, I would like to let you know that the Tribunal is very appreciative of what you have done. It needs the cooperation of all states, and it is very sensitive to the fact that you agreed to testify without any protective measures during a particularly transparent testimony, vis-à-vis the public in an institution which wishes to be as transparent as possible. The Registrar will escort you from the court. We will take a 20-minute pause and then resume in 20 minutes. When we resume I would like Mr. Harmon to tell us what is going to happen. (4.26 pm) (A short break) (4.55 pm) (Open session) (The accused entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Cayley, the following witness is protected?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. President, your Honours, learned counsel, good afternoon. The next witness is a protected witness. I have conferred with Mr. Nobilo, and he has no objection to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Could you explain what the testimony is going to be about, please? Mr. Nobilo, do you have any objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: No, Mr. President, I do not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. Cayley, you can proceed, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, your Honours, the next witness, who will be known as Witness JJ, is a Muslim male from the municipality of Kiseljak. His testimony will be divided into five discrete but interconnected sections. In the first section of his testimony he will speak to you briefly about the location of his village in the municipality of Kiseljak, the number of inhabitants prior to this war, the ethnic mix of the village. He will talk briefly about his membership of an organisation called the Patriotic League. He will explain the function and indeed the disorganisation of that particular institution. He will then speak to you about a brief membership of the Bosnian military police, his reasons for leaving, and all of this will be connected to a general description of the situation in Kiseljak in the early part of 1993. He will explain how it was common knowledge there were two streams of the HVO in Kiseljak. Finally, in this section of his testimony he will talk about increasing tension in the area and how ultimately cooperation between the Bosnian Muslims, the Bosniak Croats in his village ceased. The second section of his testimony will deal with a number of attacks that took place on 18th April 1993, in the municipality of Kiseljak. He will say how he saw the villages of Visnjica and Gomionica burning. He will speak about the attempted defence of his village and how, with agreement from the HVO not to burn any of the houses down in his village or kill any of the women and children, all the men of the village surrendered. He will explain how the HVO used the male members of his village as human shields in order to clear the rest of the village. He will explain how buses arrived in an organised convoy to remove all of the Muslim residents from his village, how an agreement was made between the HVO and a sympathetic Croat in his village for the Muslim residents to stay and how subsequently the members of the village were effectively prisoners in their own home. He will explain how on a regular basis he and other male members of the village were forced to dig trenches, how HVO soldiers came on an almost nightly basis, with black masks over their faces, robbing people's houses. He will explain what happened to one of the most valuable commodities in these villages, to the livestock, in these villages, in his village in particular. The third section of his testimony will deal with events that occurred a couple of months later, when all of the villagers were in fact forcibly removed and taken to a village (redacted). You will hear in subsequent testimony about that village. He will describe the rounding up of all the villagers. He will describe how people were led to believe by the HVO how they were to be exchanged, how members of the village were forced to hand over the keys to the domestic property, their housing and cars. He will then describe how people were tricked and in fact taken to the village of (redacted). He will describe the conditions to you in what can only be described as an HVO-created Muslim ghetto, a cross between a ghetto and a camp -- a camp without walls. He will describe the overcrowding in the ghetto. He will describe the chronic lack of food, how Muslims were regularly robbed on their way back from the town in Kiseljak in attempting to bring food to sustain the Muslim -- what can only be described as prisoners in the village. He will describe how soldiers came in the middle of the night to rob people in the village, how he went daily to dig trenches from 7.15 until 4 every day. He will describe the reasons why nobody tried to escape from this camp, this village without walls. The final part of this part of his testimony he will describe how he observed the mosque in his village -- a number of days after his arrival in (redacted), on a journey to dig trenches, he drove past in a truck the mosque in his village which he noticed had been destroyed. Finally he will speak of the main mosque in Kiseljak and how he noticed at the same time how that mosque had been destroyed. The penultimate part of his testimony will deal with a time when he was taken along with a large number of other males to the town of Kiseljak. That will deal generally with his imprisonment in the Kiseljak barracks, the absolutely appalling treatment meted out to male Muslims in those barracks, regular torture, beatings of prisoners, trench digging and the conditions while digging those trenches. He will describe how he was taken on a daily basis past the HVO main military headquarters in the barracks, to dig trenches. He will describe how, when UNHCR representatives came to the prison, prisoners were well fed for a couple of days before their arrival and moved between cells in order to create a situation which appeared to the international community was one of greater humanity, but in fact it was an illusion created by the HVO for international observers. Finally, he will speak of a particular task he was given of removing a number of the corpses of Bosnian soldiers, two of which had been decapitated, and a gruesome game of football was played with these heads in the town of Kiseljak. Eventually those heads ended up on stakes in the town. He will speak again of his time in the Kiseljak prison, of regular stealing of property from prisoners, how wealthier prisoners were taken away from captivity in order to show HVO soldiers where their valuables were hidden. Lastly, he will deal briefly with his exchange in November of 1993, and his return in fact on a visit -- he was not allowed to stay – (redacted) where he spoke to the Croat man who is now occupying his house where he and his family lived for many years. Finally he will talk about his opinions about the organisation of the campaigns against the Muslim population in the town and municipality of Kiseljak. His testimony, if I can relate it briefly, for your Honours to the indictment is relevant to count 1, persecution count, paragraphs 6 to 7, counts 8, 9 and 10, the causing of serious injury, both physically and mentally, to civilians (that is paragraph 9 of the indictment); counts 11 to 13, destruction and plunder of property, that is paragraph 10 of the indictment; count 14, destruction of institutions dedicated to religion and education, that is paragraph 11, and, finally, counts 15 to 20, which is inhumane treatment, the taking of hostages and the use of human shields -- that is paragraphs 12 to 16 of the second amended indictment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Cayley. You gave a very clear summary. If we could have Witness JJ brought in, please. (The witness entered court) WITNESS JJ

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Do you hear me.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Please identify your name -- do not state your name, just nod if this is correct. (Handed).

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Now, be seated. You are being covered by protective measures. You are going to make your statement, which is your oath, according to a sentence which is going to be given to you by the Registrar. Please read the statement.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you. Excuse us for calling you, Witness JJ, but it is for your benefit. You agreed to come to testify in the trial, which is here at the International Tribunal, of General Blaskic who is in this courtroom. Speak without fear. You are being protected by international justice. The Prosecutor told us what the main lines of your statement will be, which will make the proceedings go more smoothly. You will speak freely, and you will be guided by the Prosecutor's questions. The Prosecutor in this case is Mr. Cayley. Mr. Cayley, I give you the floor. Examined by MR. CAYLEY:

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness JJ, you are of Bosnian nationality; is that correct. Could you repeat the answer to that question? You must speak up in order to be heard.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I believe you are a former resident of the village of Hercezi, which is in the municipality of Kiseljak; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If the witness can be shown exhibit 276. Mr. Usher, if you can place that on the ELMO (Handed). If the ELMO could be illuminated. Witness JJ, can you point, please, on that map to the location of your village?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My village is over here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And if you could just point to the town of Kiseljak?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Kiseljak is here (indicates).

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the two arrows indicate the roads to Busovaca and Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, this one is the Busovaca and this one is to Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness JJ, prior to the war, approximately how many inhabitants were there of the village of Hercezi?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: About 100 to 120 inhabitants.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what was the ethnic composition of the village prior to the war?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was mixed, both Croats and Muslims lived there. We had no Serbs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, if you could just briefly tell the judges of the time commencing with your membership of the Patriotic League, through to the attack on your village on 18th April -- if you could stop at that point, and deal with a description of the Patriotic League, your time in the Bosnian Army military police and your reasons for leaving and generally describe the situation in Kiseljak during that time as you perceived it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I joined the Patriotic League because the JNA called up recruits to join the campaign in Croatia. However, we did not accept that, so I joined the Patriotic League, and, as the war spread in Bosnia, mostly in Sarajevo, which was close enough, I moved to the military police. I transferred there to the sector of Lepenica in order to protect the Muslim and the Croat population as well, because, at that time, at Koscari there were a lot of them alongside us. I left the military police, because the situation between the Croat and Muslim population was getting ever more tense. The HVO in Kiseljak did not allow passage through Kiseljak. There was some mistreatment, there was some taking away of the weapons from the Muslims, and so, out of these security reasons, I left the military police and returned to my village. In the village, we were on guard duties, night watches in order to protect ourselves against the Serbs and their possible raids at night. As far as the weapons are concerned, we had some hunting weapons. I had a pistol that I got from my father, and then we had some makeshift weapons like some explosives and such. Later, we received some weapons from the HVO after they broke into the ex-JNA barracks, collected all the weapons they found there; they gave us three or four rifles and that is what we used.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness JJ, how would you describe the level of organisation of the Patriotic League?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was no particular organisation there. It was a man from the village. We just put together a list of who was going to be on guard duty and the next day we would again agree on who was going to guard the village and that was it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you said that the situation in Kiseljak between the Muslims and the Croats got steadily worse. Were you aware in your own mind of two streams of the HVO in Kiseljak and, if you are, or were at the time, can you explain those two streams to the judges?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were two streams or factions. One was led by Raic and the other by Lujo. However, those two factions came into conflict, because Lujo's faction helped the Muslim population quite a bit -- they protected the Muslim population, so that I know that. When Lujo was killed and Marko Pecirep who was together with Lujo, and they were killed by some of Raic's soldiers, who were special units.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the attitude of Ivica Raic's faction to the Muslims in Kiseljak, in the municipality?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The position was that they did not allow us to pass through Kiseljak. When a larger number of soldiers would come to go to Koscan, individual soldiers would be disarmed, the uniform would be taken away from them, in case they had been able to acquire one.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you described nightly patrols in your village to guard against attack. Were these initially joint patrols with the Croat residents of Hercezi?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At first, there were joint guards with -- guard duties with the Croats, but as the situation in Kiseljak worsened, they separated out, but occasionally we would meet at the bridge -- we would talk, we would exchange news and things like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We can now move to the second section of your testimony. I would like you to describe to the judges the events of 18th April 1993 -- what occurred in your village and then, if you could move on through to the time when all of the residents of the village of

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On the night of 17th and 18th April, I was on guard duty until about 2 am and then went home to sleep. In the morning, my mother came in and said that the war had started, but there was Easter -- it was a Croat holiday and I thought there was some celebration going on. However I saw that Gomionica was already on fire, I saw that the shooting had started and I realised that it was no celebration, that the war had actually begun. We organised ourselves in the village. There were about 15 able-bodied men there. We split between two ends of the village; we knew what we needed to protect. However, we lost our communication with both Gomionica and Visnjica, so we did not know what was going on. As the day wore on, there was more shooting and more houses were on fire, so we gave up any resistance and we withdrew in the forest. The first two days nobody came to the village, but the third day, the HVO army arrived in the village, and we were told to surrender all weapons so that they would not torch the village, they would not kill women and children, and us as well. So that is what we did. Without firing a single bullet we surrendered all the weapons, so there was no torching and no killing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When the HVO entered your village, did they in fact clear the houses in the village and did they use the male members of the village to assist them in that? Can you explain to the court what happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: All able-bodied men were detained in the house of (redacted). We were told -- we saw a bus that was supposed to take us to the Kiseljak barracks. (redacted) (redacted) guaranteed -- he said that we had surrendered weapons, that there would be no problems and we could stay at home. So we spent two to three nights in (redacted) (redacted) house. After that, we were released to our own homes but with the proviso to report three times a day to (redacted) (redacted). I do not know -- we were supposed to report maybe so, I guess, we would not escape from the village. The rest of the time we had to be inside our houses for our safety, because a lot of the military passed through and this pair could not protect us out in the street, in the open, so we had to stay within the house -- the houses.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were the Muslim residents of the village, in effect, prisoners in their own homes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, exactly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you taken by the HVO, the male members of the village on a daily basis to perform forced labour?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Every day we were taken to the forced labour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you explain to the court where you performed that forced labour during this time, and what that forced labour was -- what you had to do for the HVO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: While we were under house arrest, we went to dig in the village of Mrakovi. We dug fox holes and trenches -- the canals which were helping them either to defend or better attack the Muslims.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: While you were still residing in Hercezi, did HVO soldiers come in the middle of the night to the village?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They came both at night and during the day. There were robberies, there were all kinds of things. Only if a neighbour would come and would not want to be recognised, he would put over his head a kind of a sock and then rob his neighbour that way and take away whatever he wanted.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were these individuals wearing HVO uniforms?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they wore uniforms and the HVO insignia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You say they wore a black stocking over their head in order for them not to be recognised by members of the village?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They surely did it for that reason, and maybe they were ashamed, too -- they were embarrassed, otherwise I do not know why else they would have put it on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened to all of the livestock in your village?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: All livestock that was in the village was taken to Kiseljak and we were told that there were strict orders from Raic that the livestock was needed for the HVO soldiers as food.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in order to make it clear for the judges, can you just tell them from your understanding, who was Ivica Raic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At that time, he was a superior of the HVO -- he was the commander.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the Kiseljak municipality?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can the ELMO be switched on again and if you could just indicate the villages that you observed on the morning of 18th April that were burning, as you saw it from Hercezi?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Can I ask what was his grade in the army, can the witness tell us?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Do you know the rank of Mr. Raic, Witness JJ?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Officer, soldier, general?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know his rank, but he was the superior person there. He led and commanded -- I do not know exactly what rank he held.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: He was the commander of a division -- of a whole division, or he acted on his own?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think he must have had someone who was commanding him, but I know that he was commanding all the units who were there in the municipality of Kiseljak.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Witness JJ, if you could just indicate to the court the villages that you observed burning on 18th April, just by simply pointing to those villages and naming them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Visnijca and Gomionica, those two villages .

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. You briefly mentioned that a message was transmitted by the HVO, that if all the men from the village surrendered the village would not be burnt down and the women and children would not be killed. Did you receive that message directly or did you hear that from somebody else?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We got this message from (redacted) who at that time, was, how shall I put it -- was our commander, kind of commander of the 15 of us, the 6 (redacted), gave that message. He was the commander of that unit who came to cleanse the village and told us to surrender weapons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the unit that had come to cleanse the village was an HVO unit; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct, that was an HVO unit. They were all (redacted). We knew all of them, we knew them well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If we could now move to the third segment of your testimony. If you could describe the time, a couple of months after 18th April when the HVO arrived in your village and rounded everybody up and took you to the village of (redacted). I would like you to describe to the judges that rounding-up process. I would like you to describe the conditions in (redacted), and I would like you to explain why you did not try to escape from that place, and, finally, if you could end that portion of your testimony at the point where you were taken to the Kiseljak barracks?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: One morning, when the able-bodied men from the village were out digging, I stayed home. I asked Pero to let me stay, because I was sick. A bus came and several small cars with the civilian and military police of the HVO police inside. They told us that we had five minutes' time to get ready, that we were going for a private, that is, that we would be taken to the Muslim side. Of course, we were glad to get out of this arrest -- house arrest -- and, if nothing else, to be spared from the daily digging. However, we could not all fit into one bus. We were told we had five minutes, but there was a policeman in front of each house, and he was hurrying us up, so we did not even have five minutes. We were boarded on the bus and driven to Kiseljak, and we moved on towards (redacted). The bus stopped, and we were told, in front of a cafeteria called Konak, that we should go to (redacted) and that we would be staying in (redacted) -- it was up to us to find accommodation, and we saw that nothing would come of the exchange, that we had been cheated. From there, with our bags, we went to (redacted), we found some small houses that were abandoned, so that the next day we saw that new buses -- fresh buses were coming from other villages such as Topole, Brnjaci, wherever there were any Muslims, they were brought there, and we realised that nothing would come of the exchange and that we would have to stay there in detention.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: (redacted), what did the HVO military police say to you in respect of your vehicles and the housing in the village?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We were told that we had to give them the keys of our houses, and our cars, which of course we did -- we gave them our keys of houses and cars.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If the ELMO could be illuminated again, please, could you point out for the judges the village of (redacted)?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is here (indicates).

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, when you were putting the marks on this map for me, you also put two broken lines at the end of the village nearest the road. What do they represent?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We marked a part of the road from Kiseljak to (redacted), which had been cleansed of Muslim inhabitants. Everything was burned and destroyed. There was no-one living there, everything had been destroyed and torched.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So, the Muslims were concentrated in the far end of the village of (redacted)?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, at the end of the village, in a valley.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you explain to the judges and describe the conditions in (redacted)?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The conditions were difficult of course, because we did not have time to take with us any food or clothing, so, for my child, which was small -- it was a baby of a few months -- I did not have time to take powdered milk and of course we did not have any real milk, because there was no livestock, so that it was indeed difficult.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many families occupied the house in which you were placed by the HVO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was not the HVO that placed us there. We put ourselves up. We just depended on what we found. In the house that I was in, there were three families, and there were, I think -- no, exactly, there were 14 of us in that house.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were the conditions generally in the village of (redacted) overcrowded?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, overcrowded. As the houses were full, people could not find any others, so they stayed in a small mosque, so that was full, too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the Muslims who were placed in (redacted) attempt to purchase food in Kiseljak?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, we were told that we could go to Caritas and that they would give us food. People went there, but what happened was that, very often, we suffered badly because some HVO soldiers would beat up a woman, take away the food, so that people preferred to go hungry than go to Caritas to get some aid from them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you required to perform forced labour in (redacted)?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We did not go for forced labour that first day only. After that, every day we had to go digging from 7 in the morning until 4, half past 4, in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what did you have to dig on behalf of the HVO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Again, we had to dig trenches, dugouts -- mostly, it was just digging.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If the witness could now be shown exhibit 68(1), 68(2) and 68(3). (Handed). Now, a number of days after you arrived in (redacted), I think you were taken to Mrakovi to dig trenches and I think you passed by the village of Hercezi; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you see the mosque?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, we passed right by the mosque -- maybe at a distance of 50 metres, the mosque is about 50 metres from the road.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does this photograph represent what you saw at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is the mosque, in the village of Hercezi.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And it had been destroyed, as is shown in this photograph?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, both the mosque and the house next to the mosque, in which the haja lived.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, if you could lift that photograph off, because the witness made a comment about the house. Could you point to the house of the Muslim priest?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, this is the house of the Muslim priest, right next to the mosque.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If the final photograph could be shown. . This is the interior of the mosque, although you would not have been able to see it from the road, but do you recognise that as being the interior of the mosque in your village?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can recognise it. I want to say that, two years ago, I entered the mosque and I buried my father there, so I actually visited the ruins -- these ruins.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If the witness could now be shown exhibit 277. (Handed). Do you recognise this photograph?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, this is the mosque in the municipality of Kiseljak.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you see this structure shortly after you arrived in (redacted) whilst being taken by the HVO to dig trenches?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We passed by this mosque on a daily basis when we were taken to dig trenches. The first time I saw it in this condition was when we were taken to (redacted) for what was supposed to be an exchange, but, really, they just changed the village in which we were staying. In no way did our way of life change.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So, it would be correct to say that a couple of months after 18th April 1993 the mosque in Kiseljak was in this condition, because you saw it like this at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At the time, it was in this condition, whereas now it is even in a worse condition.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Whilst in the village of (redacted), were Muslims again visited on a nightly basis by HVO soldiers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot really say that it was every night, but, on 90 per cent of the evenings, we were mistreated; our jewellery or money, whatever we had, depending on what one had, was taken away from us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why is it that you did not try to escape from the village of (redacted)?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A man in such a position did think about all kinds of things, even about suicide, but we were told if we were taken digging and somebody tried to escape, his wife or child would be killed, and anyway, it was impossible to escape from (redacted), because its position is such that it is surrounded by hills, surrounded again by HVO front-lines. It was impossible, and we were also threatened that, should anyone escape from trench digging, then his wife, child or mother -- whoever was left behind, whoever one had -- would be killed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, if we can move to the fourth section of your testimony. If you can tell the judges about the time when you were taken from trench digging to the barracks, the HVO barracks at Kiseljak, and if you can describe the conditions that you suffered in those barracks, the treatment meted out to the Muslim men kept at the barracks and the work that you were required to perform for the HVO whilst you were there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: One day, I was digging, as usual, every day, at Mrakovi and three HVO policemen came -- I knew one of them -- his name was Zeljo Pravdic, who called me and told me that we had to go to the barracks. He was looking for a relative of mine, to go as well, as he was not digging. We found him at (redacted) -- he was ill -- and we were taken together to the barracks. We were taken into a room, where a man was lying on the floor immobile. Later, when we asked him what was wrong, he told us that he had been beaten up and I could see that he was telling the truth, because a short while later I was taken to an office, where the prison commander was waiting -- Miro Biletic and another two HVO soldiers. Miro Pravdic asked me questions -- he was looking for weapons which we did not have, but that was an excuse for them to beat me, so I went through the same procedure as the man in the room -- I was kicked, I was hit with sticks, with fists, I fainted there in that room. When I came to, I saw that (redacted) was no longer there, so I knew that he was going through the same treatment as myself and that was in fact what happened.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you could tell the judges about the work you were required to perform on behalf of the HVO whilst you were at the Kiseljak barracks?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We did all kinds of work -- the main thing was the digging, but we also had to clean the premises where their police were -- the toilets. We had to work on a daily basis.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If the witness could be shown exhibit 278? (Handed). If it could be placed on the ELMO, please. Witness JJ, do you recognise this photograph?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you made certain marks on this photograph for me and I would be grateful if you could explain to the judges what the circles represent and, if you could, whilst identifying them, state the number of the circle at the same time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Circle number 1 is the building which had cells inside, where we were imprisoned and where the HVO military police was. Circle number 2 is the headquarters of Ivica Raic and circle number 3 is the place where we were loaded on to buses and driven to work, and this dotted line is the road along which we entered the prison and along which we went out, and we were loaded at number 3 on to trucks, and taken for forced labour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how regularly were you taken to perform forced labour while you were imprisoned at the Kiseljak barracks?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was taken every day, with the exception of five or six days, when I was beaten up so badly that even they knew that I could not go to work.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And, if you can recall, how many men gathered at that point prior to going to dig trenches?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the cell, where I was, there were between 60 and 80 of us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you can recall, how large was that cell?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were not large. I believe, under normal conditions, the area would be sufficient for 20 soldiers, or 20 prisoners -- I do not know how to express myself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You are expressing yourself just fine. Now, can you describe to the judges the hygiene conditions in this prison?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The hygiene conditions were such that we did not have water, we did not have a toilet -- we used 3-litre cans for urination and, when we needed to go to the toilet, if we did not do it while digging, sometimes people would have their bowel movements in a peace of paper, wrap it up, and then the next day, when they were taken trench digging, they would throw it away.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How much food did you get while you were imprisoned in the Kiseljak barracks?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We got a loaf of bread, which was less than one kilo and it had to be shared by 20 men.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you described to the judges at the beginning of this segment of your testimony, that you were beaten. Did there come a second occasion when you were more seriously beaten by the HVO and, if so, can you describe that occasion to the judges?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After this first time, I was beaten again very badly another time. It was about 2 after midnight when a guard, a policeman, called me out by name. He told me I had to go out to wash some cups that had been used for coffee. However, when I got outside into the corridor, the order was to: put your hands on your back, to bow your head. That same policeman, closing the door -- I was the first one, he jumped on me from behind, he kicked me in the back. Of course, I stumbled and I saw there were another five or six of them in the corridor. They started kicking me and hitting me with sticks. Then they took me into a dark room, and, when I fell to the floor, Ivo Medic, an HVO policeman, felt me along my spine, and he was hitting me, and saying that, after this, I would be -- I would have to live in a wheelchair. They went on beating me. I do not know how long this lasted, but not one of the prisoners approached me, and I could understand this, because if a prisoner helped a beaten colleague, he would be the next victim, and nobody dared to help anyone.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it the case that in fact all of those 60 to 80 men in your cell were beaten at some time while you were in the Kiseljak barracks?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was not a single person detained, be he young or old, a minor or an elderly man, a woman or a child, that was not beaten -- not once, but several times.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If the witness can be shown exhibit 279 -- Mr. President, if the interpreters are prepared to work for 5 or 10 minutes extra, I believe I can conclude the examination-in-chief this evening?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: We will ask them. I know they are very tired; I know they began at 11 o'clock. I am a bit bothered by all this. I do understand their problems, and I have empathy for them, but what I do not understand, when we have a team of interpreters who are supposed to start at 14 hours and finish at 9 o'clock, why this team began at 11. It is not their fault, but of course it does disturb our work. We would have to resume tomorrow. I have received a note from the legal officer of the Trial Chamber -- you know tomorrow the whole morning is taken by the plenary session (redacted) (redacted), together with the Presiding Judge of this Trial Chamber. We decided that we could start at 2.30 and we will vacate the Trial Chamber at 4 o'clock. In the meantime, we have to finish the examination of Witness JJ and hear the cross-examination by the Defence, which I suppose will not be too long, and also there is the ex parte hearings that have to be heard. I do not suppose they will go on too long. I assume that they are just some comments to be made. I suppose we would start at 2.30 tomorrow and go on until 4. This causes a lot of constraints for everybody, for the judges, for the interpreters and I do understand the interpreters are tired. Are the interpreters prepared to work for another 5 or 10 minutes, at least to finish with the examination-in-chief? Once again, I would like to thank you, but I would point out to the Chief Interpreter, that when teams are being set up, they have to try to keep the scheduled -- try to stay within the five or 10 minutes, preferably five, but do what you have to do and then we will start again tomorrow at 2.30.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I promise the interpreters it will be five.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness JJ, do you recognise this photograph that is in front of you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do, and very well -- it is the building of the military police, where we were detained -- rather, I was detained with others.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And, indeed, there is a sign on the side of the building which states "HVO Military Police, Kiseljak"; is that correct -- can you say "yes" or "no"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How much weight did you lose while you were imprisoned at the Kiseljak barracks?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 10 to 12 kilograms.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you explain to the judges what happened when representatives of the UNHCR visited the prison?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What happened was that we figured that this was a different world -- the food was better, but this was only that one day, and, after that, it reverted to the old ways.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And were prisoners moved in between cells in order to create an impression of more comfort -- perhaps "comfort" is not the right word but certainly to reduce the impression of overcrowding?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We were about 70 at that time -- about half of them were moved to another room, which was adjacent to this room, but this was done, of course, just to show that we had enough space there, that we were not packed like sardines, but, by the night-time, they were brought back to our room.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If the witness could be shown exhibit 280? (Handed). . Do you recognise the men in this photograph?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you explain to the judges why their trousers are so filthy dirty and ragged?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that this is the best proof of the state of hygiene there and how much we had to work. I do not think that any further comment is needed for this picture.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Prisoners who remained in the Kiseljak barracks, did you have your personal property stolen from you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were taking everything -- jackets, watches, money -- simply whoever had good quality shoes or sneakers -- they would force men to take them off and he would force you to take off the shoes that belonged to a killed Muslim fighter and you had to wear those.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, if there were any particularly wealthy prisoners that were held in the barracks, what happened to them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Would you please repeat this question?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Those prisoners who were known by the HVO to be wealthy or rich, what would the HVO do to them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were cases when they were taken out of the prison for a few hours, they would take them to his house and they would pressure him into telling them where he kept his belongings, where the money was, the gold, or valuables and, of course, after that, he would then be returned to the prison.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And this was the HVO military police?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was both the military police and I was also in a situation -- I saw when an older man was taken by a soldier in his car. He took him with him home, asking him for money and gold and then beat him up.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell the judges briefly about when you were required to move a number of corpses of Bosnian soldiers from Kiseljak to Kresevo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This was at Cimburov Brijeg. That was a hill -- since the HVO had taken a good portion of that territory around Kresevo, the prisoners up there were not able to really service that new front-line, so we were all taken up to Kresevo. I stayed for about 15 days whereas another group stayed for a full month. The first morning we dug all day, and that night we took six bodies down to Kresevo -- three of them were headless and they kicked them around like a football -- they played soccer with those heads.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: These were Bosnian soldiers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Bosnian soldiers, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If the witness can be shown exhibit -- the final exhibits 281 and 281A -- if that could be placed in front of the witness rather than placing it on the ELMO. (Handed). This is a map that you marked for me, Witness JJ. If you could explain to the judges each of the locations and what the marks represent?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The marks on the map are the places, that is, the locations where I was taken to this forced labour. Number 1 is the village of Mrakovi; number 2 is Palasko Brdo; number 3 is Cimburov Brijeg; number 4 is Dubrave, number 5 Duke; number 6, Umjece; and number 7 is going to be the Palasko Brdo and number 2 is Kiseljak -- that is beyond Kiseljak, that is in the direction of direction of Crvene Stijene, that was towards Visoko.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All those marks indicate where you were required to dig trenches until you were released in November 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, those were locations where I had to dig while I was imprisoned.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I think I am correct in saying you were exchanged in November 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, this was on 6 November 1993. I was released in such a way that I was digging at the front-lines. The food was such that I collapsed from exhaustion. I could not dig any more. I was transferred to the military hospital in Kiseljak, and they figured that I was not -- that I would not survive so I was taken to Visoko to be treated -- they thought I would need surgery, the surgery was not needed, and I just stayed on, on the Bosnian side.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You have in fact been back to Hercezi, have you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, it is impossible to return to Hercezi. I have not been back to date. I live in Visnijca.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you like to return to Hercezi?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The desire is there, and it is great. However, I am not sure that it will be realised.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: That is the end of my examination-in-chief, Mr. President. If I could apply for admission into evidence of all of the exhibits 276, 277, 278, 279, 280 and 281 and 281A.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Cayley. I would like to tell Witness JJ that he will come back, ask him to try to rest tonight, to relax a bit. You will be asked some questions tomorrow, rapidly, by the Defence, perhaps some from the judges. This will be at 2.30 tomorrow afternoon. The court stands adjourned.
